sections.title: Why relational data is different
blocks: In language and vision, a single pretrained transformer can move to a new task with little or no extra training. Relational data has no such model yet, even though most structured enterprise data lives in relational databases . The trouble is the shape of the data. A database is several tables with columns of mixed types, and primary and foreign keys link rows across tables. The signal for one prediction is spread over rows, columns, linked tables and time .

Take the question this course follows. Will Anna Müller (customer 35), a customer of the synthetic shop ShopDB, place no order in the 30 days after 2025-03-01? The customer’s own row in customers holds a name, a country, an age, a premium flag and a signup date. Most of the evidence sits in other tables: the 31 orders placed before that date, the products those orders point to, the reviews the customer wrote, and whether they went quiet in earlier months. A model has to gather that evidence across keys and respect time: to predict at a time t, it may only use rows created before t .
There are four established ways to hand such a database to a model, and each of them loses something on the way.
Four ways to hand ShopDB to a model
Each view is built from the live ShopDB around the running example. Switch tabs to compare them. RT reads the data differently from all four.

The paper concludes that none of them can be the backbone of a foundation model for relational databases . RT is designed around three principles instead. It should capture the relational structure while keeping the natural symmetries of relational data, support flexible self-supervised pretraining, and generalize zero-shot to databases with other schemas .

In one sentence: RT reads a context window of cells sampled around a seed row, and predicts the one masked cell of that row . The prediction is either a logit, for a yes/no target like churn, or a z-score, for a number . The model itself is short: once the masks are built, the path from cells to the final vectors is the 22 lines below. Chapter 13 runs this same pass again, one operation at a time, with every matrix and weight on screen.

Lines 208-214 add the column-name term, 216-224 add each token’s value term (or the learned mask vector, for the masked cell), 226-227 run the blocks, and 229 is the final RMSNorm. A decoder for the target’s type then turns the masked cell’s final vector into the prediction .

sections.title: Three ideas
blocks: The paper lists three innovations . This section shows each one on the live example.
1. Cells are tokens

RT “represents each database cell as a token, with embeddings constructed from its value, column name and table name” . A cell token is a triple (v, c, t): value, column, table . The value goes through a small encoder for its type: number, text, datetime or boolean. The column and table enter together as the text embedding of the phrase “<column> of <table>”, made by a frozen sentence encoder . Key columns become links instead of tokens, and missing values are skipped .
What becomes of every cell of the seed row and its parent row
Keys turn into links, missing values disappear, and every other cell becomes one token labeled with its phrase.

Why cells and not rows? A cell is the unit every database shares, whatever its schema. And once cells are tokens, any prediction task becomes “fill in this masked cell”, the same objective RT is pretrained on .

In the paper’s notation a token’s embedding is x=Wd r+W Eschema(c,t): the value r, projected by a matrix for its data type d, plus a projection of the phrase’s text embedding. For a masked cell, a learned mask vector takes the place of the value term . In the forward pass shown earlier, each projected term also passes through its own RMSNorm before the terms are added . Chapter 8 works through the formula with live numbers.
2. The task is a table

A forecasting task such as churn has no column in the database: its labels must be computed from future rows . RT stores them in a task table, one row per entity and timestamp, holding a foreign key to the entity, the timestamp and the label . With task-table prompting, that table is attached to the database. Only one task table is active at a time, and its rows are the seed rows. To the model it is just another table .

Attaching the task table pays off when the sampler explores around the seed. The entity’s earlier task rows are children of the entity’s row, so they enter the context like any other rows, labels included . These are in-context labels. Unlike few-shot prompting, nobody has to pick labeled examples for the model: the labels arrive because they sit in rows linked to the entity . In the live context, 12 earlier churn labels of Anna are visible.
Every customer-churn row of customer 35, on a time line
Rows dated after the seed never reach its context . Hover a marker for its split and label.
3. Structure lives in the attention masks

The tokens themselves say nothing about how rows are linked. That structure enters through relational attention: each block runs four attention layers with the same arithmetic and different masks. Column attention connects cells of the same column, feature attention connects a cell to its own row and the rows it points to, neighbor attention connects it to the rows that point to its row, and full attention connects everything . There are no positional encodings, so the order of tables, rows and columns does not matter .
Who the masked cell may attend to, in each layer
One strip per mask, one mark per token of the live context, in sequence order; colored marks are the allowed keys. Hover a strip to name a token.

On this context the masked cell sees 13 tokens through column attention, 7 tokens through feature attention, none through neighbor attention and all 128 through full attention. Information from rows farther away also arrives along the links, over more than one layer. For example, the customer’s cells read the orders that point to them in a neighbor layer, and the masked cell reads the customer’s cells in the next block’s feature layer . Chapters 9 to 11 follow those paths.
Each sublayer normalizes the stream, computes its update and adds it back (a pre-norm residual), in the order column, feature, neighbor, full, then the MLP .

sections.title: What zero-shot means here
blocks: The paper defines zero-shot relational learning as “predicting new targets on a new RDB with a new schema, without weight updates. Information about the new RDB is available only at inference time, solely through the context window” . To test this, the authors pretrain one model per target database, on all the tasks of all the other databases: a leave-one-database-out protocol . This site runs one such split. It pretrains on SchoolDB, RacingDB and ForumDB and holds out ShopDB.
Leave one database out, on this site

At test time nothing is retrained. For each seed row of the new database the sampler builds a context, one forward pass runs with frozen weights, and the output at the masked cell is the prediction . Whatever the model learns about ShopDB, it learns from that window: the cell values, the column and table names as text, which cells share a column, a row or a link, and the past labels of the task that happen to be in it .
Ask the frozen model about another seed row
Each pick samples that row’s context and runs one forward pass with the same weights. It does not change the rest of the course unless you press the button.

sections.title: Tables, rows, columns, cells
blocks: A relational database is a collection of tables linked through relationships between them. Each table is made of rows, and every row is a set of cells, one for each column . That small vocabulary is all RT needs, and it takes it literally: one cell becomes one token .

Our running database is ShopDB, a synthetic online shop with 4 tables: 80 customers, 30 products, 1,286 orders and 303 reviews, recorded from 2024-01-07 to 2025-06-30. It plays the part of a database the model has never seen: the miniature RT on this site was pretrained on three other synthetic databases, and ShopDB was held out (chapter 14).
Anatomy of a table: a few orders rows
Pick a word to see what it refers to. The rows are real rows of the live database.

sections.title: The ShopDB schema
blocks: A database’s schema lists its tables with their columns and data types, together with the relational structure . In the diagram below each card is a table. A key icon marks the primary key and a link icon a foreign key, with an arrow to the table it references. Every other column is a feature column, drawn with its type glyph: # for numbers, Aa for text, a clock for datetimes and a toggle for booleans. The time column is a feature column too, marked with a time tag.
ShopDB: tables, keys and links
Hover a table to trace its links; click or tap it to open it in the table browser below.

In the diagram, customers and products have no foreign keys: nothing points out of them. orders (→ customers, products) and reviews (→ customers, products) hold foreign keys, and each also has a time column. Events point to the entities they involve.

Schemas differ from one database to the next. That is why the paper argues that pretraining needs a schema-agnostic architecture, one that takes in the multi-table structure through attention masks . RT never receives this diagram as such. It sees cells, each labeled with its column and table name, plus the links between rows (chapters 4, 5 and 9).
how a table declares its keys and time column

Each table file carries three metadata entries: pkey_col, fkey_col_to_pkey_table and time_col. They tell preprocessing which column is the primary key, which columns are foreign keys and to which table, and which column is the time column .

Table browser
The number on the left of each row is its position, and it equals the primary key: customers[35] has customer_id = 35. RT relies on that convention, as the next section shows.

ShopDB has a few gaps on purpose: age is missing for 10 of 80 customers and review_text is missing for 23 of 303 reviews. RT neither imputes nor masks a missing value. The cell simply produces no token, so that row has one token fewer .

sections.title: Keys link rows: F→P and P→F
blocks: A table usually has a primary key, the column that identifies each row, and some tables also have foreign keys that reference the primary keys of other tables. These references turn the database into a graph. A link from a foreign key to the primary key it references is an F→P link, and the same link seen from the other end is a P→F link .

In ShopDB, an order’s customer_id and product_id are foreign keys. Each order therefore has two F→P links, up to its customer and its product. Seen from the other end, each customer and each product has P→F links down to its orders and reviews. The row a foreign key points to is the parent; the rows pointing to a row are its children .
Link explorer
Parents sit above the focus row and children below; the graph draws the same rows, with arrows from child to parent (F→P) . A row has few parents, but it can have many children.

Walk around for a moment and an asymmetry shows up. A row has at most one parent per foreign-key column, so no ShopDB row has more than 2. Children are another story: products[4] (27-inch Monitor) is referenced by 313 orders and 67 reviews. The number of F→P links is limited by the number of foreign-key columns, while P→F links have unbounded degree .
Parents per row, at most
one per foreign-key column (orders, reviews)
Children per row, at most
products[4], no limit in principle

The paper turns this asymmetry into its sampling rule. RT never reads a whole database at once. For each prediction it starts from one row, the seed row, and collects the cells of nearby rows into a context window by walking the key links outward . We call the part of RT that does this walk the sampler (chapter 6). Parent rows usually hold important features (an order links to its customer and its product), and there are few of them, so the sampler follows every F→P link right away, without subsampling. Children are different: their signal usually comes from looking at many of them together, and each extra child adds less. So the sampler follows at most w children of any row, a limit called the width bound .
The dashed line marks the width bound w: when RT builds a context, it follows at most w children of a row (chapter 6). The bars count every child ever written, before any time filter.

Lines 439-442: the primary-key column is skipped, so it makes no token and no edge. For a foreign key, a null value is skipped (462-464), the parent is ptable_offset + val (477), and its index is pushed onto the row’s parent list f2p_nbr_idxs (479). The branch ends with a continue (line 532, below this excerpt), so a key never makes a cell .
one foreign-key value, two edges
The F→P edge is stored on the child; the P→F edge is appended to the parent’s adjacency list and carries the child’s table and timestamp, which the sampler reads later .

sections.title: Feature columns and key columns
blocks: Each token is one cell, but not every cell becomes a token. Once a row is selected, “all its non-missing feature cells (i.e., cells not from primary- or foreign-key columns)” enter the context . Chapter 6 covers two small exceptions: a context that fills up, and columns that would give away the answer of an autocomplete task .

A feature column holds information about the row. A key column only says which row is which and which rows are linked. Feature values come in four types: numbers, text, datetimes and booleans . A boolean becomes 0 or 1 and is then normalized like a number (chapter 4) . ShopDB’s boolean columns are customers.is_premium and reviews.verified.
What RT keeps of a row
Split the row and watch where each cell goes. Try a row with a missing value from the menu.

The paper names two costs of this choice . RT does not use the names of primary-key and foreign-key columns, which often carry useful meaning. And it cannot tell apart two foreign keys that point to the same table. The paper’s example is a product table with both buyer_id and seller_id referencing a user table: the model cannot tell which user bought and which sold.
Two foreign keys into the same table

No token carries a foreign-key column name: a column name reaches the model only through a cell’s column-name embedding , and key columns make no cells. Only the parent list and the edges remain. ShopDB never has this problem: no table has two foreign keys into the same table.
how preprocessing splits a row

The primary-key column is skipped outright . A foreign-key column makes no token either: each non-null value becomes an entry in the row’s parent list plus a pair of edges . Every remaining column is a feature column, and each of its non-missing cells becomes a cell record , typed by how the column is stored . Chapter 4 follows those records into numbers.

Integer and 32-bit float values are cast to Float64 and become numbers. A null matches the empty arm on line 552 and leaves no trace. The boolean arm shown here is one of four (number, datetime and text follow in lines 565-605) .

sections.title: Time
blocks: Many relational databases are temporal: timestamp columns record when rows are created . A table may declare one time column. In ShopDB, orders have order_time and reviews have review_time. customers and products have none. The customers table does have a datetime column, signup_date, but it is an ordinary feature and not the table’s time column.
The time column is still a feature column: order_time becomes a datetime token like any other . It has a second job as well: it gives the row a timestamp, which the sampler uses.

The paper explains why time matters: “if we want to predict whether a user will buy an item at time t, the model must only use information available before t, otherwise it risks temporal leakage” . Below are all time-stamped rows linked to customers[35] (Anna Müller). The accent line is the prediction time t, set to the simulation seed’s timestamp, 2025-03-01. Everything to its right is the future.
Activity of customers[35] over time
Each mark is one row. Drag on the chart or use the slider to move t; hover a mark for details, click it to make it the focus row.

Inside RT, the sampler enforces this rule in a narrower form. When it visits a row, it first drops the children whose timestamp is later than the seed’s; a child with the same timestamp stays. Then it keeps at most w of the children that remain, chosen uniformly at random (all of them if there are w or fewer) . Parents are never checked . In ShopDB, customers and products have no foreign key, so their rows are never anyone’s child: they enter a context only as the seed or as a parent, and the time rule never removes them. Chapter 6 runs the whole algorithm step by step.
how the sampler applies the time rule
Lines 406-408 push every parent with no time test. Lines 421-424 drop a child whose timestamp is later than the seed’s .

sections.title: The database as a graph
blocks: Put all the links together and the database becomes a graph. Relational deep learning (RDL) makes this explicit: it represents a database as a relational entity graph, “a temporal, heterogeneous graph where each table is a node-type, each row an individual node, and every primary-foreign key relationship an edge” . The first models ran graph neural networks directly on that graph; later work refined their message passing and moved to transformers .
The neighborhood of customers[35] as an entity graph
Each node is one row, colored and shaped by its table; each arrow is one foreign-key link, child to parent. The dashed rings mark the hop distance from the center row. Click a node to recenter.

The paper’s objection to these architectures is that they are schema-specific, so they cannot be pretrained and fine-tuned across databases with different structures . RT keeps the links but changes the unit. The paper describes its own design like this: “our model uses a cell-level representation of the entire database and employs attention masks to directly represent the foreign-key structure” .
Same rows, two representations

Switch to the cell view. Each row breaks into its feature cells, its key cells make no token, and the links stay as structure. This is not yet a context window: chapter 6 decides which rows enter one.

That is the raw material RT works with: a pool of cells, each knowing its value, its column and its table, plus the links between rows. The next chapter adds the last ingredient, the prediction task. A forecasting task arrives as one more table attached to the database; an autocomplete task just masks a cell of an existing row .

sections.title: Every task is “fill in the masked cell”
blocks: RT has a single job: predict the value of a masked cell. The paper calls this masked token prediction: “predict the value of a masked cell in the database, conditioned on the rest of the observed database” . Two broad families of tasks on relational data fit this mould :
Autocomplete: the missing value belongs to a column that already exists, such as the star rating of a review.
Forecasting: the value is about the future, such as whether a customer will order again. Such targets “do not exist in the original database and must be constructed from future rows” .
Two ways a cell can be missing

Live ShopDB rows. Left: the rating of review 151 is hidden, and the leakage column that would reveal it is dropped. Right: customer 35’s churn label is stored in no ShopDB table; it is computed from the orders after t.

Either way, each training or evaluation example masks exactly one cell, the target cell of its seed row. Every other cell that enters the context stays visible , except that autocomplete tasks first drop their leakage columns (section 4) . The type of the target cell decides the loss: a boolean target is trained as binary classification, a numeric one as regression . The paper masks only these two kinds of cell, “as RelBench tasks are either binary classification or regression” .

sections.title: Building customer-churn, step by step
blocks: A forecasting label needs a home, since no table stores it. RT takes the answer from RelBench: a task table, which “stores the forecasting labels, together with foreign keys linking to the relevant entities (e.g., user IDs or item IDs) and a timestamp specifying the prediction horizon” .

ShopDB’s version is customer-churn: will the customer place no order in the next 30 days? Each row has three columns: a timestamp t, a foreign key customer_id, and the label churn. Like RelBench task tables, it has no primary key . The label summarizes the future window (t, t + Δ], here with Δ = 30 days .

sections.title: Three splits, one table
blocks: RelBench gives every forecasting task three splits : Train rows at the training timestamps, Val rows at the validation cutoff (2025-03-01) and Test rows at the test cutoff (2025-04-15). Each split is stored as its own file , and RT gives each one its own block of node indices . Test rows keep their labels in the file. When a Test row is the seed, its label is masked like any seed’s, and evaluation compares the prediction with the true value .

Choose where a seed row sits. The sampler skips a task row only if its timestamp is later than the seed’s, so rows at the same timestamp pass . Passing this filter does not put a row in the context: that depends on the search and on L (chapter 6).

Move the seed to Test. The Val rows are now earlier than the seed, so they pass the filter, and a Test prediction can use Val labels as context. Rows at the seed’s own timestamp pass as well (the hatched bar), so a Val seed can see other customers’ Val labels, and a Test seed other customers’ Test labels .

To RT, the three splits are one logical table. All three get the task’s name, and the split only sets a table type . Each name is turned into an index once, so the three splits share one table-name index and one index per column . Live from the preprocessed ShopDB:

Because the splits share one table, past rows of the task, from any split, look to the model like ordinary rows of that table. The sampler reaches them through the customer, and their label cells stay unmasked. They are the in-context labels : “while task rows provide ‘in-context labels’, our setting is not few-shot as explicit subgraph-label pairs are not required” .

In your live context (customer-churn, L = 128, w = 16 scaled down) the seed is customer #35 Anna Müller’s Val row. The seed’s own customer contributes 12 visible past labels, and other customers contribute 0. The search did reach 3 other customers, but only far from the seed (5 hops), and the 128 slots filled up with closer rows before their task rows were taken . Chapter 6 shows the order in which the search takes rows.

For comparison, on RelBench the paper counts about 19 past labels of the target entity per 1024-cell context for rel-f1 driver-dnf and about 4 for rel-amazon user-churn, with few or none from other entities .

sections.title: Regression targets and autocomplete
blocks: A regression task: product-sales

Forecasting labels need not be booleans. product-sales asks how many units of a product will be ordered in (t, t + 30 d]. The recipe is the same as for churn with a different aggregation: add up the quantities of the window’s orders instead of checking that there are none. The label is a number, so this is regression, trained with a Huber loss on the label’s z-score . The z-score uses the Train split’s mean and standard deviation for Val and Test rows too .
Hover, tap or focus a bar to see the orders it sums. A click pins it, and the arrow keys move between windows. Pick any product (the choice applies only to this chapter).
The official code lists each of the paper’s tasks as a tuple of database, table, target column and leakage columns. A forecasting task names its task table, and its leakage list is empty.
Autocomplete: the target is an existing column

Autocomplete needs no new table: “sampling starts from the masked database row” . The seed is a database row and the target is one of its cells. Every row whose target cell is present is a seed . An autocomplete task has no Train, Val or Test split: the code always takes its seeds from the whole database table, from every period .

Autocomplete hides a trap: other columns of the same row can give the answer away. ShopDB’s review 1 reads “Terrible quality, broke within days.” and its rating is 1. So each autocomplete task lists leakage columns, which the sampler drops on the fly . For the paper’s rel-amazon rating task they are review_text and summary ; ShopDB’s rating task drops review_text. The drop applies to the seed row and to any row with exactly the seed’s timestamp. Other reviews in the context keep their text .
An autocomplete seed: which cells become tokens

Pick a review and a task. The right side samples a real context with your L, w and RNG seed, then shows the seed row’s tokens. With reviews.rating the seed’s own review_text never enters the context. With reviews.verified nothing is dropped, as in the paper’s rel-amazon review.verified task .

No task rows appear in an autocomplete context, because the sampler enters a task table only from a seed of that same table (section 5) . The in-context labels are the visible target values of other rows in the same table, such as other reviews of the same product. scaled down
In the official code
The rating of a rel-amazon review would leak through its text and summary, so both are dropped.

sections.title: Task-table prompting
blocks: How does the model know which task it is solving? Through task-table prompting, the first of RT’s two innovations in input representation (the second, cell-level tokenization, is the subject of chapter 7) . “For each task,” the paper writes, “we attach a dedicated task table to the database. Only one task table is active at a time, ensuring that sampling is task-specific. Rows from the task table serve as seed rows for context construction, and from the model’s perspective task tables are treated as ordinary relational tables” .
Attaching a task table to ShopDB
Attach either forecasting task. The task table joins the schema like any other table, with one foreign key to its entity, and its rows become children of that entity.

Why a table and not a special input? Because a table puts the task in the same input space as pretraining: the model reads it through the same cells, column names and links as the rest of the database. In the paper’s words, task-table prompting “augments the database input with task-specific context, enabling zero-shot predictions across diverse schemas” , that is, predictions on a new database without weight updates . And since the task’s past rows carry their labels, the table also shows the model what answers look like for this entity and its neighbors .

In the code, “only one task table is active” is a rule in the sampler. Preprocessing indexes every task table of the database , but the sampler follows a link into a task table only when the seed belongs to that same table . A customer-churn seed never pulls in product-sales rows, and an autocomplete seed, being a database row, pulls in no task rows at all.
table_name_idx is shared by Train, Val and Test, so past rows of the same task pass the first test from any split; the second test is the temporal filter.

sections.title: What the model sees of a task row
blocks: Strip away the table and a task row is small. After preprocessing it has exactly two tokens: the timestamp cell (a datetime) and the label cell (a boolean or a number). The foreign key makes no token. It becomes a link: the entity’s node index goes into the row’s f2p_nbr_idxs list .
A task row becomes two tokens

From your live context: customer-churn, seed node 2406, L = 128, w = 16 scaled down. Hover a token for the value stored for the model. Both rows have the same two tokens; only the seed’s label is replaced by the mask.

The seed row carries no marker of its own. It is special only because its label cell is the one masked token . The next chapter turns all these rows into numbers: which cells become tokens, and how each value is normalized (chapter 4).

sections.title: From rows to cells
blocks: Before the Relational Transformer sees anything, a preprocessing program runs once per database. It turns the database into one long list of rows, and every row into a few typed cells, with numbers, booleans and datetimes already normalized. This chapter follows that program on ShopDB, value by value.
How every row of every table, task splits included, gets one global node index.
Which values become cells: keys turn into links and missing values vanish.
How the physical dtype alone decides a cell’s semantic type.
How numbers, booleans and datetimes are z-scored, and which rows feed the statistics.
What one cell looks like after preprocessing, slot by slot.

sections.title: One program, run before everything else
blocks: RT never reads raw tables while it trains or predicts. Instead, the official code first runs a Rust program, pre.rs, once per database. It writes what the sampler will need: one record per row, the links between rows, every feature value already converted into numbers, and one string table that a separate script embeds with the frozen text encoder . The program works in three passes.
Read the tables
Every parquet file, database tables first, then task splits. Each file gets a node_idx_offset, which fixes the global index of its rows.
read 1st here
Compute column statistics
Mean and standard deviation per number and boolean column; one global pair for all datetimes.
read 3rd here
Build the node vector
Table by table, column by column: links and edges from foreign keys, one typed cell per non-missing feature value (z-scored with the pass-2 statistics), and the string table.
read 2nd here
This chapter takes them in the order that is easiest to learn: the index space first, then which values become cells, then the statistics that normalize them.

Everything below is computed live in your browser on ShopDB (e-commerce) by a TypeScript mirror of pre.rs. It produces the same rows, links, cells and statistics; only bookkeeping, such as the numbering of the string table, differs. The figures follow the simulation settings in the top bar, so the seed row you see here is the same one every other chapter uses: row 32 of customer-churn:Val, which points at customers[35] (Anna Müller).

sections.title: One index space for every row
blocks: pre.rs gives every row of every table a single integer, its global node index. “Every table” includes the task tables: the Train, Val and Test splits of each forecasting task are files of their own, and their rows are numbered in the same space as the database rows .

Rows are numbered in the order pre.rs reads the files: first the database tables (db/*.parquet), then the task files (tasks/<task>/<split>.parquet), each group sorted alphabetically by path . That is why orders comes before products here, although the schema lists them the other way round, and why a task’s test split comes before its train split: test < train < val.

A file’s offset is the number of rows read before it, so a row’s index is node_idx_offset + its row position . The offsets are saved in table_info.json under keys like customers:Db or product-sales:Val .
ShopDB: 2,826 rows in 10 files, one index space

Press play to replay pass 1: pre.rs reads the files one by one, and each file’s offset is the running row count. Segments are colored by table, and all task tables share magenta. The accent pin is the live seed row; the other pin follows the row picked below.

Why one shared space? The attention masks and the sampler compare rows only through these integers (“is this token in the same row as that one?”, “is that row one of my parents?”) , and one integer per row answers those questions the same way for every table. Autocomplete tasks add nothing to the bar: their seeds are ordinary database rows .
Lines 93-95 skip link-prediction tasks (their directory names carry two extra dashes), which RT does not handle.

sections.title: Keys become links, missing values vanish
blocks: Inside a table, pre.rs walks the columns in their stored order and applies three rules to every value :
The primary key produces nothing: no cell and no edge . Its value is the row position, which the node index already encodes.

A foreign key produces no cell either. Its value becomes a link: the parent’s node index joins the row’s f2p_nbr_idxs, and the parent gets an edge back . This is also where the row’s timestamp is set, from its time column .
Every other value is a feature value. If it is present, it becomes one cell record. If it is missing, it produces nothing: the model never sees a placeholder or an imputed value .

The paper says the same in one line: once a row is selected, “all its non-missing feature cells (i.e., cells not from primary- or foreign-key columns) are included in the context” . Key columns shape the graph; only feature columns carry values.
One row through pass 3, column by column

Press play (or step) to watch each value land in its lane. The node record at the bottom fills up as pre.rs goes. The signed numbers in the Cells lane are z-scores from pass 2 (see Normalization below): roughly, how many standard deviations a value sits above or below its column’s average. Picking another row here does not change the global seed.

These cell records are not tokens yet. A cell becomes a token only when the sampler picks its row for a context window (chapter 6). Even then, a task can make the sampler leave a cell out: it may name leakage columns, whose cells are skipped for the seed row and for every row with the seed’s timestamp (in ShopDB, reviews.rating drops review_text). That rule belongs to the task, so pre.rs keeps those cells like any other. Across the whole database, the three rules of pre.rs add up as follows.

sections.title: Four semantic types, read off the dtype
blocks: Every cell carries a semantic type. There are four, with fixed codes from the SemType enum: Number = 0, Text = 1, DateTime = 2, Boolean = 3 . The model later loops over the types in exactly this order to pick an encoder, a mask vector and a decoder for each cell .
The type comes from the column’s physical dtype and from nothing else :
dtype → semantic type, with every feature column of ShopDB
Task-table columns appear once: the three splits share one table name and one column phrase.

pre.rs does no semantic inference. A string column is Text even when it really holds a category, so a country code is embedded as a short string. An integer column that is not declared as a key is a Number: a 1-to-5 rating is z-scored like a price, and so would be an integer id that nobody declared as a key .

Boolean is a type of its own: the model gives it its own encoder, mask vector and decoder, as it does for numbers . The type also decides the loss: a masked boolean cell is trained with binary cross-entropy, a masked number with Huber (chapter 12) . So a binary task is trained as classification only when its label is stored as a boolean. In ShopDB, the label churn of customer-churn is a boolean column from the start. RelBench stores some binary labels as 0/1 integers, so pre.rs casts those label columns to Boolean when it reads them .

sections.title: Normalization: three kinds of z-score
blocks: Numbers, booleans and datetimes are stored as z-scores: subtract a mean, divide by a standard deviation. Text is not normalized. It is stored as an index into the database’s string table, and the frozen text encoder embeds it later . Nothing is clipped, so an outlier keeps its large z-score. The paper writes the shared formula as
The three kinds differ in which values feed μ and σ.
Numbers: one μ and σ per column
For each number column, pre.rs computes the mean μ and the standard deviation σ over the values that are present, then stores every value v as (v − μ)/σ .

The z-score is a new ruler under the same data: 0 sits on the mean and one unit is one σ (the shaded band is μ ± σ). Bars are colored by table. Default probe: the seed’s own customer, where it applies.

The paper does not say why it standardizes. A likely reason (our reading) is the encoder: one shared Linear(1, d) per type, with d = 256 in the paper and 64 here scaled down, reads every number column of every database . Standardized inputs show it how unusual a value is within its column, on the same scale whether the column holds prices or ages.
Booleans: true lands above zero

Booleans use the same formula after casting true → 1 and false → 0 . With a share p of trues, μ = p, so true becomes (1 − μ)/σ, which is positive, and false becomes −μ/σ, which is negative. The values are not ±1: they depend on how common true is, and a rare true sits far out on the positive side.

The rest of the code relies on the sign alone. The loss for a boolean target is binary cross-entropy against 1{z > 0}, and evaluation turns labels back into int(z > 0) . A stored value can sit anywhere on its side of zero and still give back the right label .
Where true and false land on the z axis
Filled dot: true; hollow dot: false. Move the slider, or use the chips, to change how many values are true (n stays fixed). The dashed dots keep the real column for comparison.
Datetimes: one clock for the whole database

Datetimes get no per-column statistics. Instead pre.rs pools every datetime value of every table, task splits included, and computes a single mean μT and standard deviation σT for the whole database .
Each row is one datetime column of one table file. The accent triangle marked “seed” on the z ruler is the seed row’s timestamp.

The paper asks to “normalize globally” without giving a reason . One effect is plain from the code: the same instant gets the same value in every column. A task row’s timestamp and an order’s time sit on one scale, so the model can compare them directly.
Task labels: Train statistics for every split

Task tables get one extra step. pre.rs first computes stats for every file separately, then overwrites the Val and Test splits’ stats with the same task’s Train stats . A Val label is therefore normalized with the Train mean and σ, never with its own.
The split’s own label distribution differs from Train’s, but the μ and σ used are Train’s, so the same label is stored as the same value in every split.

For task labels the code does what the paper asks: statistics “computed on the training split” . The labels being evaluated do not shape their own encoding, and because the three splits share one table name and one column phrase (chapter 3), a Train label seen in the context and the Val label being predicted are on the same scale .

sections.title: Pick a cell, see its encoding
blocks: This panel puts the whole chapter together. Click any cell of any table, task splits included, and the panel follows it through pre.rs: its role, its semantic type, the statistics that normalize it, the record slots it fills, and the embedding term that will read it in chapter 8.
The cell inspector
Picking cells here is local to this figure; the global seed does not change.

Two details stand out in the slot view. First, every cell record has all four value slots, but only the one that matches its type is filled, and a non-text cell stores text index 0 . The model multiplies each type’s term by a 0/1 gate on the sem type, so the empty slots never contribute . Second, the seed’s own label is stored like any other cell, because preprocessing knows nothing about masking. The sampler marks it as the target later, and the model then swaps its value term for a learned mask vector .

sections.title: Text and schema semantics
blocks: RT reads the names in a database. Every cell token carries a vector for the phrase “column of table”, made by a frozen sentence encoder, and every text value is embedded the same way. This chapter opens those vectors and asks how much they help a model move to a database it has never seen.
Which strings RT embeds, and the exact phrase “<col> of <table>”
What a real 384-dimensional all-MiniLM-L12-v2 vector looks like, and why its length is 1
How close the column phrases of ShopDB are to those of the pretraining databases
What it means that a text value is embedded without its column, and that the encoder is frozen
What the paper’s ablations say about the value of names
seed customer-churn:Val[32] → customers[35] (Anna Müller) · target phrase churn of customer-churn · 128 tokens use 17 distinct phrases scaled down

sections.title: Every cell carries the name of its column
blocks: RT describes a cell as a triple (v,c,t): its value, its column name and its table name . The value is normalized (numbers, dates and booleans; chapter 4) or embedded (text; Step 5) and becomes the token’s value term. The two names are joined into a short English phrase, “<column_name> of <table_name>” , and a frozen text encoder embeds it. The paper’s examples are “price of product” and “age of user”, and it calls this schema semantics .

Every cell token carries the vector of its column phrase, whatever its type: a number, a date, a boolean, a string, and the masked target too . In the live context the target is the cell churn of customer-churn, so that phrase’s vector is part of the token the model must fill in.
The column phrases of a database

Every column phrase of the database, grouped by table. Struck-through phrases belong to key columns: they get a string index but never a cell. Bars count the tokens of the live context that carry each phrase. Switching the database here does not change the live simulation.

Why a phrase rather than a column id? One of the paper’s three design principles is to “enable zero-shot generalization across heterogeneous schemas” . An integer id means nothing outside its own database, while a phrase can be compared across databases. “age of customers” in ShopDB and “age of students” in SchoolDB are different columns, but they share words, and the encoder places them close together: cosine 0.53, against 0.13 for an average pair of phrases from different databases. Step 3 measures such closeness for every pair.

The primary-key and foreign-key columns get a phrase as well, because preprocessing makes a phrase for every column before it looks at the column’s role . But a primary key produces no cell, and a foreign key only becomes a link to the parent row . So customer_id of orders has a vector that no token ever uses. The paper lists this among RT’s limitations: it “does not incorporate the names of primary-key and foreign-key columns, which often carry useful semantics” .

The table name reaches a token only through the phrase. Each token also carries its table’s index, table_name_idx, but as a plain integer that the column mask compares (chapter 9) . No vector is ever looked up from it .
One string table per database

Preprocessing collects every string of a database into one list, in order of first appearance: table names, column phrases and each distinct string value . It writes the list out as text.json . Identical strings share one index, and so one vector .
The string table of ShopDB

The first entries of the string table, in index order. Preprocessing walks table by table and column by column, so table names, phrases and values interleave. The order itself means nothing: the model only compares indices for equality or uses them to fetch a string’s vector .
text_to_idx is the database’s single string table. A string seen before keeps its index.

sections.title: A real 384-dimensional vector
blocks: The text encoder is a small MiniLM model from the SentenceTransformers library , namely sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L12-v2 . It is a 12-layer BERT with hidden size 384 and a lower-casing WordPiece tokenizer . Its pipeline has three modules, Transformer → mean pooling → Normalize . In words: split the string into wordpieces, run all 12 layers to get one 384-dimensional vector per wordpiece, average them, and divide the average by its length.
Inside the encoder, for one string

Any of the 722 strings embedded offline for the four databases. The wordpieces come from the real tokenizer; the vector is the stored one. Hover a cell to read a dimension. The comparison rows show that the cosine of two unit vectors is the sum of their 384 element-wise products.

Words missing from the 30,522-entry vocabulary are split into smaller pieces, and every piece after the first is marked “##”; the target phrase becomes 9 wordpieces, [CLS] chu ##rn of customer - chu ##rn [SEP]. The encoder still returns one vector for the whole string. The tokenizer also adds a [CLS] token at the start and a [SEP] token at the end, and the average includes both.

Because of the final Normalize step, every vector has length 1 . All the information is in the direction, and the cosine similarity of two strings is simply their dot product. Step 3 uses that measure.

sections.title: Similarity across databases
blocks: Names could help a pretrained model on a new database if the new database’s phrases land near phrases of related meaning in the pretraining databases. The paper does not test this idea, but you can check here whether the phrases do land close. The matrix compares every ShopDB phrase that can reach a token (rows) with those of the other three databases (columns). Each cell is a cosine computed in your browser from the stored vectors.
Cosine similarity: ShopDB phrases vs the pretraining databases

Color runs from 0 to the largest cosine shown, rounded up to the next 0.1. A ring marks each row’s best match. Rows are grouped by table. Columns are grouped by database and then by table, with each table’s name and color above its group.

Take the label of the live task, churn of customer-churn. You might expect its closest relatives to be the labels of the pretraining databases’ tasks. That is not the case here: the nearest pretraining phrase is reputation of users (cosine 0.385), a feature rather than a label; next comes engaged of user-engagement (0.318). The average over all 46 pretraining phrases is 0.133. This is where each of their task labels ranks:

The encoder knows only language. It places a phrase by its words and their everyday meaning, and the table name inside every phrase pulls on it as well. Over all four databases, two phrases of the same table average a cosine of 0.560, two phrases from different tables of one database 0.225, and two phrases from different databases 0.128.

RT never compares phrases of two databases directly, because every context comes from a single database. It only receives these vectors as input and passes all of them through the same learned projection. Any benefit from similar vectors has to come through that shared projection, and pretraining decides what to make of them.

sections.title: A map of every column phrase
blocks: To see all 99 column phrases of the four databases at once, we project their vectors onto the two directions along which they vary most (a principal component analysis, computed offline from the same stored vectors). Two axes cannot hold 384 dimensions: they keep 18% of the variance, so points that look close are not always near neighbors. Pin a phrase to draw its true nearest neighbors, measured in all 384 dimensions.
Column phrases of the four databases, 2-D PCA

Color and shape mark the database. Hollow markers are key columns, which never reach a token. Dashed lines join the pinned phrase to its five nearest phrases in 384-d. Click a database chip to hide it.

In this projection, the key-column phrases (the “…_id of …” ones) sit at an average PC 1 of +0.35, the other phrases at −0.18. The full 384-d vectors agree that they form a group: two key-column phrases average a cosine of 0.436, a key-column phrase and another phrase 0.156, two other phrases 0.163. Along PC 2 the databases spread out, from SchoolDB (average +0.32) to ShopDB (−0.29). This matches the averages of Step 3: two phrases of one database are closer than two phrases from different databases, probably because the phrases of a database share its table names and domain words. RT never computes this map. It is only a window onto the vectors RT receives.

sections.title: Text cells: the raw value, nothing else
blocks: String values go through the same encoder, applied to the raw string with nothing added: r=Etext(v) . Preprocessing adds the value string itself to the string table , the encoder embeds it with the rest of the list , and the sampler copies its vector into the token’s text_values . The column never becomes part of the string . In the live context, the customer’s value “DE” is embedded as exactly that string.
Two vectors per text token
Pick a text cell of the live context. The token holds two separate rows of the string table: its column phrase and its raw value.

So a text cell gets its column context only from the separate column term . Inside the model, each of the two vectors passes through its own linear layer and RMSNorm, and the results are added ; chapter 8 follows that sum.
One string, one index, in every column

In SchoolDB, “Computer Science” is a value of both program of students and department of courses. The string table holds it once, as text[28], so both cells carry the same value vector and differ only in their column vectors (cosine 0.552).
5 such strings across the four databases: “Computer Science”, “Biology”, “History”, “Mathematics”, “Economics”

Cells that are not text still fill text_values. Preprocessing gives them text index 0 , which in ShopDB is the table name “customers”, and the sampler copies that vector as well. It only fills the slot: the model multiplies the term by zero, because the token’s sem type is not text .
The encoder reads at most 128 wordpieces of a string and cuts the rest . The longest string in the four databases here has 21 wordpieces, so nothing is cut.
val is the cell’s string as it is: no column name, no table name. col_name_idx (line 603) is stored separately.

sections.title: Why names matter
blocks: The paper tests the value of names directly. It shuffles the column and table names in the context and measures performance with the same pretrained checkpoints . In zero-shot evaluation it shuffles the names in each sampled input context. For fine-tuning, it trains the model to convergence on contexts shuffled the same way . The same experiment also removes two kinds of labels from the context, which gives a yardstick for the names.
Mean over the RelBench tasks for each context ablation (paper Table 4, p.9)

In the paper’s words, “the model indeed leverages table/column names for zero-shot transfer, as wrong names lead to consistent degradation. After full fine-tuning, context ablations have little effect” (the exception it names is self labels on regression) . On average, zero-shot AUROC falls by 0.6 points and R² by 2.3 points. Removing the target entity’s past labels costs 16.3 and 28.3, and the paper concludes that “zero-shot transfer is driven primarily by the model’s ability to leverage past labels of the target entity” . Names are a consistent but smaller signal. They probably matter less after fine-tuning because a fine-tuned model has seen many labeled examples of the task and can learn what each column means from its values. A zero-shot model has to rely more on what the names say.

The mean hides how much the tasks differ. In zero-shot, shuffling lowers the score on 7 of the 10 binary tasks and 7 of the 8 regression tasks. The largest drops are rel-hm user-churn (−2.8 AUROC) and rel-stack post-votes (−4.9 R²), while rel-stack user-engage gains +3.0 .
The paper’s conclusion ranks what drives zero-shot transfer . Names come fourth of five, after the target entity’s past labels, which fits the gap between their two rows in Table 4:
forecasting from the target entity’s past task rows;
column attention;
feature attention, in the same and in parent tables;
schema semantics from table and column names;
in-context learning from other entities’ task rows.
Not lexical copying

Could the model simply match identical column names across databases? The paper checks with the Jaccard overlap of the column names of two databases: the number of shared names divided by the number of distinct names in the two together, ∣A∩B∣ / ∣A∪B∣. Between RelBench databases it is tiny, at most 0.043 (rel-amazon vs rel-hm) . The paper concludes that “RT’s zero-shot generalization cannot be attributed to lexical similarity. Instead, the model must learn to recognize and exploit structural relational patterns” .
Column-name overlap (Jaccard) between databases

Jaccard overlap = shared column names / distinct column names of the two databases. The first grid has the paper’s numbers. The second computes the same statistic live on this site’s four toy databases, over the columns of their database tables (keys included, task tables left out). Hover a cell for the counts and the shared names.

That still leaves open how names help, and two readings fit the results. Names may carry meaning across databases through the encoder, as Step 3 measures. Or they may mainly tell columns apart within one context, as the note in Step 1 describes. The shuffle removes both, so Table 4 cannot separate them.

sections.title: The encoder is frozen
blocks: RT never runs its text encoder while it trains or predicts. embed.py embeds the whole string table once and writes the vectors to a file . The sampler maps that file into memory and copies rows by index . So no gradient can reach the encoder. The first trainable parameters on the text path are two linear maps from 384 to d, enc_dict["col_name"] and enc_dict["text"], each followed by its own RMSNorm .
Where the text vectors come from, and where learning starts

The paper describes it as “a frozen text encoder” . Keeping it frozen has three consequences. Training never pays for the encoder, since each step reads precomputed rows. A new database needs one pass of the encoder over its strings and no change to RT. And a string has the same vector in every database, so the similarities of Step 3 stay fixed and pretraining can learn to use them.
The learned part, live
encode() runs the pipeline of Step 2 and returns one 384-dimensional unit vector per string.

blocks: RT never reads a whole database. For each prediction it gathers L cells around the row to predict, with a bounded breadth-first search. This chapter runs the released sampler on the live seed, one decision at a time.

sections.title: Why sample?
blocks: RT reads a database as a set of cell tokens, and a whole database does not fit in one sequence. ShopDB (e-commerce) is tiny by RelBench standards, yet the tables this task’s sampler may enter hold 7,019 feature cells. So for every prediction RT builds a short sequence around one seed row: the context window of L cells . Here the seed row is customer-churn Val row 32 (customer 35, 2025-03-01), and its masked cell is the label to predict.

Which L cells? The authors follow “the intuition that most relevant information lies within a few hops of the seed row when following F→P and P→F links, and that lower hops are more informative than higher hops” . A plain search over those hops quickly collects more than L cells. The chart counts the cells within k hops of the seed, and already at 2 hops there are more than L = 128.

sections.title: The algorithm, one decision at a time
blocks: The paper describes the sampler as a breadth-first search with three changes: all parent rows (F→P) are always included, child rows (P→F) are subsampled with a BFS width bound w, and rows with timestamps later than the seed row are excluded. Once a row is selected, its non-missing feature cells are added to the context .

The released implementation, rustler/src/fly.rs, keeps the frontier in two structures: an F→P stack for parent rows and a list of P→F depth buckets for child rows . Every frontier entry carries a depth label, one more than the depth of the row that pushed it . A row is checked against the visited set only when it comes off the frontier, so the same row can wait in the frontier more than once. Every copy after the first is skipped .

sections.title: Four rules worth remembering
blocks: Without the bookkeeping, the released sampler comes down to four rules, including the temporal filter and the width bound w. Each card shows its rule at work in the context above, and “Show me” moves the replay to that moment.
Each rule differs a little from the paper’s description, and each card says how. The released model was trained with the code, so the course follows the code .
Parents first, never filtered

As long as the F→P stack is not empty, the sampler pops its top entry, without any random choice. Parents skip both the time filter and the width bound, and the last foreign key pushed is followed first.
51 parent pushes, 52 stack pops (38 of them already visited). order 70 pushed customer 35 then product 4; product 4 was on top, so it was popped first and visited.
Children only if not later than the seed

A P→F child is skipped only when both timestamps exist and the child’s is later than the seed’s. Equal timestamps pass, and so do rows without a timestamp. The comparison is always with the seed’s timestamp, whichever row is being expanded.
263 child rows skipped as too late. First one: order 967 at 2025-03-05, after the seed’s 2025-03-01.
At most w DB children per row; task rows never subsampled

If more than w of a row’s DB children pass the time filter, the sampler keeps a uniform random w of them (without replacement). Children from the seed’s task table that pass the time filter all enter the frontier.
The bound fired 11 times; the largest cut: product 4 had 277 DB children after the time filter, 16 kept. 50 customer-churn rows entered the frontier without any subsampling.
Stop at exactly L cells
The loop breaks as soon as the L-th token is written, even in the middle of a row. If the frontier empties first, the rest is padding.
Full at L = 128: customer 44 was cut after 1 of its 4 cells.
Autocomplete tasks add one more filter: their leakage columns are skipped for the seed row and for rows with the seed’s timestamp . Forecasting tasks such as customer-churn drop no columns .

sections.title: In-context labels
blocks: The task table is attached to the database as an ordinary table , so the search can walk into it. The path is short: the seed row pushes its entity onto the stack (depth 1), and the entity’s children go to bucket 2. Those children are the entity’s DB rows, time-filtered and cut to w, and the entity’s rows in the task table (any split) whose timestamp is not later than the seed’s. The task rows are never cut to w . Their label cells stay visible, which makes them in-context labels.

The paper does not count this as few-shot prompting: “While task rows provide ‘in-context labels’, our setting is not few-shot as explicit subgraph-label pairs are not required” . The labels reach the model as ordinary cells of the context.
In the context of customer-churn Val row 32 (customer 35, 2025-03-01), customer 35 contributes 12 self labels, its own past churn values, and other entities contribute 0.
Labels the model can read, on a time axis
Top: label rows by time; everything right of the seed line is later than the seed and is never sampled . Bottom: the same label cells among all L tokens.

Other entities’ labels arrive by longer paths, for example entity → one of its transactions → the product it points to (F→P) → another transaction of that product → its customer (F→P) → that customer’s task rows . Each hop adds one to the depth label, and the lowest bucket is always drawn first, so these rows wait until the shallower buckets are empty . With w = 16 this context holds none, so the figures offer a second context of the same seed: with w = 3, every bucket is smaller, and the search reaches other entities within L = 128 cells.
How each label entered the context
For every label row of the context, the path through which the search visited it, drawn with foreign-key arrows (child → parent).

Which task rows can appear depends on the seed’s split. All three splits share one table name, so the task-table test lets every split through, and the time filter keeps every row with a timestamp no later than the seed’s :
a Train seed sees Train rows up to its own timestamp;
a Val seed sees all Train rows, plus other entities’ Val rows at the same timestamp;
a Test seed sees Train and Val rows, plus other entities’ Test rows at the same timestamp.
Visibility of customer-churn rows by seed split
Your seed is a Val row. A seed’s own row is the masked target; the rows of other entities at the same timestamp are the “same horizon” rows.
How many labels does the paper see?

For scale, the paper counts the labels in the 1024-cell contexts of its tasks. Two rel-trial tasks, study-outcome and study-adverse, get no labels at all, and zero-shot AUROC on study-outcome is 51.8, close to random .

Self labels are the main driver of zero-shot transfer. Removing them drops the paper’s mean zero-shot AUROC from 70.1 to 53.8 and R² from 22.8 to −5.5. Removing other-entity labels changes little (70.6 AUROC, 22.9 R²) . In the authors’ words, “zero-shot transfer is driven primarily by the model’s ability to leverage past labels of the target entity” .

Two mechanisms shape these counts. First, a bucket is drawn uniformly, so the self labels in bucket 2 compete with the entity’s DB children for the early positions. A larger w puts more DB children in that bucket, and a small L can fill up before every self label is drawn . Second, a smaller w keeps every bucket smaller, so the search gets to the deeper buckets, where other entities’ rows live, after fewer cells .

What does a shorter context cost? The paper varied L at inference for a model pretrained at L = 1024 and found that “RT’s performance degrades gracefully, showing a drop of only 4% absolute AUROC and 7% absolute R² with 25% lower time and 20% lower memory” (Fig. 4, from L = 1024 down to 256). blocks: The sampler hands the model L positions: up to L cells, plus padding if it runs out of rows first. Each cell fills one position of a batch dictionary, where it is stored as a few integer ids, a type, a value and some flags. This chapter goes through that record field by field, then checks two properties on the live context: exactly one cell is masked, and the order of the cells does not matter.

sections.title: The batch dictionary
blocks: The sampler of chapter 6 writes the context into parallel arrays: one array per field, one slot per position . Every slot starts as padding , and each emitted cell fills its position in every array . The model receives these arrays as tensors : [B, S] for ids, types and flags, [B, S, 1] for the scalar values, [B, S, 5] for the parent lists and [B, S, 384] for the text embeddings. This dictionary of tensors is the batch dictionary .

B is the number of sequences in a batch (32 per GPU in the paper’s runs) and S is the context length L . One sequence is one context window, so on this page B = 1 and S = 128. Each position holds one cell token or padding. Open any position below to see its record.
The batch dictionary of the live context: 128 positions

Top: one square per position, in the order the sampler emitted the cells. Middle: where the inspected token comes from, and every field the model receives for it. Bottom: the whole batch dictionary as one table, one row per position (open it with the toggle). The inspected token is shared with the embedding, masks and attention chapters.

The figure sorts the fields into four groups. The ids say which cell a token is: its row (node_idxs), its parent rows (f2p_nbr_idxs), its table and its column (table_name_idxs, col_name_idxs). The four attention masks are built from these ids and is_padding, and from nothing else . The content fields say what the cell holds: the embedding of its column phrase, its semantic type and one value slot per type, all read by the input embedding . Three flags mark the masked target and the padding. The last group holds is_task_nodes and class_value_idxs, which the sampler writes and the paper-era model never reads .

One name can mislead. The batch field masks marks the single hidden cell (Step 3). The four attention masks of chapter 9 are a different thing: S × S tables of allowed pairs, built from the ids . In the figure, the tag “attention masks” marks the fields those tables read.

Every token carries four value slots, one per semantic type. The types are number, text, datetime and boolean, numbered 0 to 3 in sem_types . Each type has its own encoder, normalization, mask vector and decoder . Only the slot that matches the token’s type counts: the code computes every type’s value term and multiplies the others by 0 . The unused slots hold filler: 0 for the scalar types and, for text_values, the embedding of the first string in the database’s string table (here “customers”) .
One vector per field, with one slot per position of the batch. The last member, true_batch_size, holds a single number for the whole batch.
seq_i is the next free position. The row-level fields (node, parents, table) are copied from the node for every one of its cells.

sections.title: Rows are not tokens, cells are
blocks: RT samples rows but tokenizes cells: “each database cell is modeled as an individual token” . Once the sampler selects a row, each of its non-missing feature cells enters the context as its own token . Only the last row of a full context can be cut short (Step 5). In the live context, orders[70] becomes 3 tokens.

Ids tie a row’s tokens back together. Each token repeats its row’s node_idxs, f2p_nbr_idxs and table_name_idxs . The feature mask uses the shared node id to let the cells of a row read each other, and the parent ids to let them read their parent rows . The neighbor mask uses the same parent ids in the other direction . Without its row’s id and parents, a token could not take part in those layers.
One row in, k tokens out

Top: the raw row, column by column, and what becomes of each value. Bottom: the row’s tokens as the model receives them. Shaded bars are the row-level fields, written again for every cell; the per-cell fields differ from token to token. The masked target still stores its label (lock icon), which the input embedding gates out (Step 3). E(“…”) is the frozen MiniLM embedding of a string (chapter 5). Click a token number to inspect it in Step 1.

The key columns never become tokens. The primary key column is skipped , and the row’s node id takes its place. Node ids number every row of the database in one sequence: each table gets an offset, the number of rows in the tables loaded before it , and a row’s node id is that offset plus its position . Keys in RelBench-style data are 0 … n−1 in row order , so a foreign key value plus the parent table’s offset is the parent’s node id, and that id goes into f2p_nbr_idxs . A missing value produces no token at all .
The parent list

f2p_nbr_idxs always has five slots, because no row may have more than five parents . The row’s parents fill the first slots in foreign-key column order , and the other slots keep −1 . The list names all of the row’s parents, whether or not they made it into the context. A parent can only change attention if some of its cells are present .

In practice the parents are almost always there. The sampler visits a row’s parents, and their parents in turn, before any child row . A listed parent ends up without tokens only if the context fills up at L first, or if the parent row has no non-missing feature cell to emit . In the live context, every parent listed by any token is in the context.

sections.title: Exactly one masked cell
blocks: Exactly one token of a context has masks = true: the target cell of the seed row. The sampler sets is_target when the row is the seed and the column is the target column, and copies it into masks . Nothing is masked at random, and training and evaluation build their sequences the same way . Every other cell is visible, including other rows’ values of the target column: the in-context labels of chapter 6 (here 12 labels of the seed’s own entity and none of other entities).
The masks field of the live context
The array exactly as the model receives it: one boolean per position. Hover a cell to see which token it belongs to. The single true entry is the seed row’s target cell .

The masked token stays in the sequence. It keeps its row and parent ids, its column phrase and its type, so the model knows which column of which table it must fill, and in which row . Only the value term of its input embedding changes: in place of the encoded value, the model adds a learned mask vector for the cell’s type . Chapter 8 computes it with real numbers.
The masked target next to a visible label of the same column

Left: the target, customer-churn:Val[32]. Right: a past label of the same entity, customer-churn:Train[564] = false. Table, column and type match, so both tokens get the same column-name term and the same encoder. They differ in row id. Of the flags the model reads, only masks differs, and it swaps the value term for the mask vector . Click a column header to inspect that token in Step 1.
The label is still in the arrays

The sampler writes the value of every emitted cell, the target included . So the true label of the seed row (churn = false) sits in the target token’s boolean_values slot, in plain sight. The model still cannot read it. The input embedding computes this value’s term and then multiplies it by the gate [sem = t ∧ ¬mask ∧ ¬pad], which is 0 for the target . The square brackets are a 0/1 switch: 1 if the condition inside holds, 0 otherwise. The stored label is used in only two places: the loss takes it as its target , and evaluation reads it as the label for the metrics .
Try it: replace the stored label and run the model again. The rerun computes every value term from the arrays, the hidden label included, and multiplies each one by its gate, as the code does.
Experiment: overwrite the hidden label

The forward pass runs again in your browser on the same 128 tokens, with only the target’s stored value replaced. At every position, the value term of every type is computed from its slot (the replaced label included), multiplied by its gate and added up , and the result passes through the four blocks. The prediction is read at the masked position , and the loss takes the stored value as its target . The bottom panel opens up the target’s input embedding.

The prediction stays the same to the last bit, while the loss can change. For a boolean target the loss reads only the sign of the stored value, 1{z > 0}, so any positive number counts as “true” . The masked cell’s value is hidden from the model but still there to grade it .
Line 219 keeps a value term only where the token is not masked and not padding. Line 223 adds the mask vector exactly where it is masked.
y is the same value array the input gate ignored; sem_type_mask keeps only the masked position.

sections.title: No positional encodings
blocks: A language model must tell “dog bites man” from “man bites dog”, so it adds positional encodings to its tokens. RT leaves them out on purpose: “To preserve the natural symmetries of relational data, RT does not incorporate positional encodings” . A table has no first row and no first column, and the paper wants a model that is “invariant to permutations of rows, columns, and tables” .

Nothing in the code depends on where a token sits. Its input vector is computed from its own fields only (column phrase, type, value, and the mask and padding flags), never from its index . The four attention masks compare only ids and padding flags . Shuffle the tokens, and each one gets the same input vector and the same set of allowed keys as before, at a new index. Write the shuffle as a permutation matrix P acting on the rows of the token matrix X: the masks M become PMP⊤, and the final hidden states H are permuted the same way :
Shuffle the inputs, and the outputs come out shuffled the same way, each one unchanged.

The hidden states are equivariant: each one moves with its token. The prediction is read at the target, wherever it lands, so it is invariant. The model cannot tell in which order the sampler wrote the cells. Shuffle the live context below and run the model again to see it.
Experiment: shuffle the tokens, run the model again

Each square is one token (color = table, “?” = the masked target). Shuffling moves the squares to random positions: the token arrays are permuted, the four masks are rebuilt from the permuted ids , and the full forward pass runs again in your browser. Adding the same numbers in a different order can change the last bits of a float, so a tiny |Δ| here is rounding. Focus the squares and use the arrow keys to follow one token.

sections.title: Padding
blocks: Every sequence in a batch has the same length, so the sampler allocates all the slots up front and gives each one padding defaults: node −1, parents −1, table and column 0, every value 0, is_padding = true . Emitting a cell overwrites its slot and sets is_padding = false . A context ends in one of two ways . Either the sampler reaches exactly L cells and stops, even in the middle of a row , or the frontier runs out of rows first and the remaining slots stay padding.
So the last row of a full context can lose some of its cells. It happens in the live context: the last row, customers[44], kept 1 of its 4 cells.
Padding: the slots the sampler never wrote

Top: the is_padding array and the tokens of a context that ran out of rows. Left: one padding slot, every field at its default. Right: what the model does with it, computed from the real weights and masks of this context.

Padding never touches the real tokens. Every attention mask requires that neither token be padding , and every term of the input embedding is multiplied by ¬is_padding , so a padding slot enters as 0 and stays 0 through every block . The figure’s last check shows the result: the same cells give the same prediction with or without the padding slots around them .

sections.title: The token embedding
blocks: Before any attention happens, every cell token becomes one vector of d numbers, x₀. It is the sum of two parts: a term that says which column of which table the cell belongs to, and a term that says what value it holds. The masked target gets a trainable mask vector in place of its value. This chapter computes x₀ for the live context, number by number.

What RMSNorm does, and why its ε shortens small inputs such as the column projection
Why every number column shares one encoder, and what the masked target’s vector still knows

sections.title: Two terms per token
blocks: The previous chapter turned every cell into a cell token: a column phrase, a semantic type, a stored value and a few integer ids . The ids only steer the attention masks of the next chapter. Everything the transformer knows about a cell’s content enters through one vector per token, the input embedding xi∈Rd, with d = 64 here and 256 in the paper .
The code builds it as follows :
Read it one piece at a time.

The column term says where the cell lives. ci is the frozen MiniLM embedding of its column phrase “<column> of <table>”, for example “churn of customer-churn” . One linear layer Wcol is shared by every column of every table.

The value term says what the cell holds. vi(t) is the value slot of type t: a single z-score for numbers, datetimes and booleans, and the 384-d MiniLM embedding of the string for text . Every cell has all four slots filled, and the gate keeps only the slot of the cell’s own type . Each type has its own linear layer Wt and its own RMSNorm.
The mask vector mt takes the value term’s place for the masked target. It is a trainable parameter, one per type, and is added as is, with no RMSNorm .
The square brackets are 0/1 gates. For a real token exactly one of the eight value-side gates is 1. For a padding token every gate is 0, the column gate included, so its x₀ is the zero vector .

Stages ③ and ⑥ are RMSNorms. An RMSNorm divides a vector by its root mean square, plus a small constant ε inside the square root, and multiplies it by a learned gain γ . Step 3 covers it in detail; for now, the panel beside each norm lists the numbers it uses.

The figure opens on the token you last inspected (the masked target by default) and plays once when it scrolls into view. Replay it, or switch between the presets and compare: two cells of the same column get the same column term, and a text value goes through MiniLM on its own, without its column name . For the masked target, stages ⑤ and ⑥ are skipped and its mask vector goes straight into the sum.
Compute x₀ for one token of the live context

Pick any token: click a square, or a preset; in the strip the arrow keys move and Enter picks. The seven stages follow model.py:208-224, with the weights of the checkpoint this page runs.
