sections.title: RMSNorm, and why its ε matters here
blocks: Each projection in the embedding is followed by an RMSNorm. It divides a vector by its root mean square and then multiplies dimension j by a learned gain γj :

RMSNorm does not subtract the mean and has no bias. With γ = 1, which is how every gain starts , the output keeps the input’s direction and has a root mean square close to 1, unless the input is tiny.

The small constant ε keeps the division safe when the input is close to zero. In RT, ε = 2⁻⁷ ≈ 0.0078 , which is large enough to matter when the input itself is short. Drag x into the shaded ε zone of the figure below and the output falls short of the circle.
RMSNorm in two dimensions: drag the input
Around the origin, magnified ×7

The output y is computed with the engine’s own RMSNorm kernel at d = 2. The dashed curve is where y lands when ε is negligible: the circle of radius √2 (rms = 1), stretched by γ. The shaded disk is the ε zone, where mean(x²) < ε and ε is most of the sum under the square root; the magnified view shows it at a readable size. Drag x into it, move it with the arrow keys after focusing the handle (Shift for bigger steps), or try the column-projection preset. The plane widens when a γ needs more room.

In d dimensions the circle becomes a sphere. With γ = 1 the output length is ∥y∥=d⋅r/r2+ε, where r is the input’s root mean square. When r2≫ε that is d, 8 here and 16 in the paper. When r2 is comparable to ε, the output stays shorter, because RMSNorm can scale a vector up by at most 1/ε≈11.3. And RMSNorm(0⃗)=0⃗ exactly.
Where ε takes over, with the real inputs of the five RMSNorms

Top: the rms of RMSNorm’s output (before γ) as a function of the rms of its input. Bottom: every distinct input of the live forward pass, one dot each, placed by its rms. Left of √ε, ε is more than half of the sum under the root and the output keeps less than 71% of its full length; well to the right (r ≫ √ε) it reaches full length. Hover or tap a dot for its numbers; click it (or focus it and press Enter) to inspect that token in Step 2.

Now the real inputs. In the checkpoint this page runs, the column projection Wcolc+bcol has a median mean square of 0.0028 over the 17 column phrases of this context, and all 17 of them are below ε = 0.0078. For a typical phrase, ε makes up 74% of the sum under the square root, so the column terms come out about 3.3 long, while number value terms reach about 7.1.

In this checkpoint a number value term is about 2.2 times as long as a column term, so the value dominates x₀. Two cells with the same z in different columns start out with similar x₀ (Step 4 measures how similar), and the attention layers have to tell them apart by the shorter column component.

The column projection’s mean square is already below ε at initialization, in our model and in the paper’s alike. PyTorch draws every weight and bias of nn.Linear(384, d) uniformly from ±1/384 , and c has length 1 . Each output dimension then has E[xj2]=(∥c∥2+1)/(3⋅384)=1/576≈0.0017, about 0.22 ε, whatever d is.
The gains γ are the only parameters of an RMSNorm. The embedding has five of them, one per projection, each with 64 entries .
The five learned gains γ, one dot per dimension
Each RMSNorm multiplies its output by its own γ (64 numbers), which starts at 1 in every dimension (the dashed line). Training moved them in our mini model; this is the checkpoint the page runs.

sections.title: One encoder per type, shared by every column
blocks: A number, a datetime or a boolean enters as one scalar z, the z-score computed in preprocessing . Its encoder is nn.Linear(1, d): one weight column wt∈Rd and a bias bt . So the value term is

As z changes, z wt+bt moves along a straight line in Rd. RMSNorm pushes every point of that line onto the sphere of radius √d (nearly, because of ε), and γ stretches the result. All values of one type therefore lie on a single one-dimensional curve .

Encoders belong to types, and every column of a type shares one. Age of customers, price of products, quantity of orders and rating of reviews all go through enc_dict["number"] . Two cells with the same z get exactly the same value term, whichever column they come from. What tells them apart in x₀ is the column term .
Move a value along its type’s curve: RMSNorm_number(z·w + b)

The curve is RMSNorm_number(z·w + b) for z from −3 to 3, computed with the weights of the checkpoint this page runs and drawn in its own two main directions (PCA, 100% of its variance). Hollow dots: every distinct stored value of the selected column; hover, tap or focus one for its value, click or press Enter to move there. × marks the limits z → ±∞. Every number column of every table lands on this same curve.

Drawing the curve in two dimensions loses nothing. z wt+bt always lies in the plane spanned by wt and bt; RMSNorm only slides each point along its own ray, and γ is a linear map. So the whole curve lies in one plane, and its first two principal directions capture all of it. As z runs from −∞ to +∞, the direction of z wt+bt turns from −wt to +wt. Before γ the curve is half a circle of radius about √d, and γ stretches it into half an ellipse.

The value term sees only the z-score, and a z-score counts standard deviations of its own column . So z = 0.5 means “half a standard deviation above the mean age” in one column and “half a standard deviation above the mean price” in another, and the column term has to carry the difference. For very large |z| the bias becomes negligible next to z wt, so the curve flattens out toward the two points marked × in the figure, as its cosine chart shows. Extreme values of one type all look alike.

Text is different. Its encoder is nn.Linear(384, d) applied to the string’s MiniLM vector, so text values do not share one curve; each distinct string is its own point . Like the column term, it starts from a unit-length MiniLM vector , and the figure in Step 3 shows where this context’s text values land relative to √ε.

sections.title: The mask vector
blocks: The seed row’s target cell is the only masked token in a context . Its value term is replaced by mt, a trainable vector of the target’s type, created as nn.Parameter(torch.randn(d_model)) . It skips both the linear layer and the RMSNorm .

The masked token still knows a lot. Its column term names the column and the table, its mask vector names the type, and its ids tie it to its row and to the entity it is about . What it lacks is its value, and the attention layers have to infer that from the rest of the context.
The four mask vectors, and what the masked target still knows

Left: the four mask vectors of the checkpoint this page runs, on one shared color scale, each compared with its starting value. Right: the live masked target, and what the code does with its hidden label.

The label itself is still in the batch. The sampler writes the true value into the target’s slot like any other cell, and only is_targets and masks mark it . The gate ¬maski keeps it out of x₀; the loss reads it later as the training target .

blocks: Each RT block runs four attention layers with the same arithmetic, each with its own weights and its own normalization. What sets them apart is a boolean mask that decides which token may look at which. This chapter builds the four masks for the live context and shows what each one lets through.

sections.title: Attention with a mask
blocks: Inside every attention layer, RT computes standard scaled dot-product attention. Each token’s query vector is compared with every key vector, the scores pass through a softmax, and the resulting weights average the value vectors . Each of the four layers has its own query, key, value and output weights and its own RMSNorm , but what makes them behave differently is the attention mask M∈{0,1}n×n: M[q,k]=1 means that token q may attend to token k, and 0 means it cannot .

You may know masks from GPT-style language models, which use the causal mask Mcausal[q,k]=1{k≤q} so that no token reads the tokens after it . RT has no causal mask. Its attention is bidirectional, and its masks are built from row, column and table ids, so they say nothing about token order . They encode how the cells relate to each other in the database.

The paper calls the column, feature and neighbor layers the Relational Attention layers, and this chapter calls their masks the three relational masks. The fourth layer, full attention (the paper also says global attention), lets every token read every other one .
Scaled dot-product attention with masking, as written in the paper.

The mask is applied before the softmax. A blocked pair gets the score −∞, and e−∞=0, so the softmax shares all of the weight among the allowed keys as if the blocked ones did not exist. Rows are queries and columns are keys, and every matrix in this chapter is drawn that way.

The figure uses the real scores of the trained mini model at the masked target. You can pick any of the three relational layers (Step 2 defines them); for now, watch only what happens to the blocked keys. Tokens are labeled row·column: val32 is the seed row customer-churn:Val[32] and c35 is customers[35].
Where the masked target’s attention goes, with real scores from the trained mini model
scaled down

Query: the masked target (token #1, val32·churn). The raw scores are q·k/√d_head, with d_head = 16 here and 32 in the paper . Switching block or head changes how the weight is split among the allowed keys, but not which keys are allowed: every block and every head uses the same mask . Those keys always get 100% of the weight.
The Python code never writes the −∞ itself. Each layer passes its mask to PyTorch’s FlexAttention, and the kernel sets the blocked scores to −∞ .
flex_attention applies the default scale 1/√E with E = d_head, and treats a 0 in the block mask as −∞ (spec §6.1).

The four attention masks of the live context

Rows are queries, columns are keys; a filled square means the query may attend to that key. The colored strips along both axes give each token’s table (key below), in emission order, so the blocks you see are rows and tables. Hover any square to compare that one pair in all four masks; click to pin the query (it carries over to the next chapters). The pinned query’s row is framed in violet.

Its diagram is a small excerpt of the real context, picked to show that layer, with the live mask applied to those tokens: lines run into the query from every key it may read.
Each diagram is an excerpt of the 128 non-padding tokens of the live context (L = 128 here, 1024 in the paper).
scaled down
Column attention
M[q,k]=1{Col(k)=Col(q)}
query: the masked target · excerpt: 26 of 128 live tokens
“Column attention helps model the distribution of values in each column.”

The masked churn cell may read the 12 other cells of its column, and these are exactly the visible labels of the task in this context: 12 from customers[35]’s own past rows and 0 from other entities (by split: 12 Train). M[q,k]=1{Row(q)∈OutLinks(k)}

blocks: The masks differ widely in density. In the live context of 128 positions, full attention allows every one of the 16,384 ordered pairs. The relational masks allow only a small share of the 16,384: column 9.3%, feature 6.0%, neighbor 3.6%. The paper implements the layers “with sparse attention masks, and compiled to efficient FlashAttention-based kernels using FlexAttention” .
Allowed pairs per mask in the live context

Bars: the share of all 16,384 ordered pairs (S = 128) that each mask allows, on a fixed 0-100% axis; the count of allowed pairs follows each mask’s name. Keys per query are over the 128 non-padding queries. The neighbor mask is the only one with empty rows.

sections.title: Details that matter
blocks: The AND with “not padding”

When the sampler runs out of rows before L, the remaining positions are padding: node id −1, parent list [−1, −1, −1, −1, −1], every other field at its default . Left alone, those −1s would match each other. A real row with fewer than five parents has −1 slots in its parent list, so the test “key row ∈ query’s parents” would count every padding token as a parent. The code therefore ANDs every mask with pad[q,k]=¬ is_padding[q]∧¬ is_padding[k] . The full mask is nothing but pad.
Why the masks are ANDed with “not padding” (the toy context of Step 7: 19 cells and 5 padding tokens)

Left: the mask the code builds, (same_node | kv_in_f2p) & pad. Right: the same expression without & pad, evaluated on the raw ids (padding has node −1 and parents −1×5). The five padding tokens are the last rows and columns (gray strips). Without the AND, 24 of the 24 query rows change; the changed pairs are outlined in red. Where the labels do not fit (narrow screens), the axes show token positions instead.
With the AND in place, a padding query has an all-zero row in every mask, and no query ever reads a padding key.
An empty row gives exactly zero

For a query that is not padding, the column, feature and full rows always contain at least the query itself, so they are never empty. Only a neighbor row can be empty, when no row in the context points to the query’s row. In ShopDB that holds for every task row, every row of orders and reviews (no table has a foreign key to them) and any customer or product row whose child rows did not make it into the context. A query with no allowed key has nothing to average, and FlexAttention outputs exactly 0 for it . Because Wo has no bias, the update added to the residual stream is 0 as well, and the token passes through the sublayer unchanged. The check below runs on the live forward pass:
max |update| = 0 at 85 empty-neighbor tokens, all 4 blocks
other tokens: smallest max |update| 0.4022
scaled down
Neighbor is feature’s parent part, transposed

The feature mask has two parts: “same row” and “the key’s row is one of my parents”. The neighbor mask asks the reverse question: “the query’s row is one of the key’s parents” . Swapping the roles of query and key is a transpose, so neighbor is exactly the parent part of feature, flipped across the diagonal . In the feature layer information flows from parent to child, and in the neighbor layer it flows back from child to parent.
Neighbor is the feature mask’s parent part, transposed

Left: kv_in_f2p & pad, the part of the feature mask where the key’s row is a parent of the query’s row . Flipping it across the diagonal swaps query and key, which is exactly q_in_f2p & pad . First 40 tokens of the live context shown; the check below covers all 16,384 pairs.
The column test also checks the table

The paper writes the column mask as a single condition, 1{Col(k)=Col(q)} . The code compares two ids, col_name_idxs and table_name_idxs . Both say the same thing, because a column id already names its table: it points to the phrase “<col> of <table>”. These ids also decide which cells count as one column. Train, Val and Test task rows carry the same table name, so they share both ids, and the labels of every split meet in a single column group .
One mask for all heads

All heads of a layer share one mask. The code builds it without a head dimension (H=None, line 96), so it applies to every head . Each head can learn to weigh the allowed keys differently, but every head is allowed the same keys.
Built once, used by every block

The masks depend only on ids, so the forward pass builds them once, before the first block, and passes the same four masks to all 12 blocks of the paper model (4 blocks here) . Inside a block the layers run in the order Column → Feature → Neighbor → Full, and each one picks its own mask .

sections.title: Inside one attention sublayer
blocks: The four kinds of attention layer in RT run the same computation, each with its own weights. What sets them apart is the mask, which decides which token may read which. This chapter follows one token through one attention sublayer of the trained mini model, with its real numbers, from the normalized input to the residual update. Then it shows the attention patterns of every layer and head.
The seven steps of a masked multi-head attention sublayer, with live numbers
How 4 heads split a 64-dimensional query into slices of 16, and where the factor 1/√16 comes from
Why a blocked key gets exactly zero weight, and why a query with no allowed key passes through unchanged

sections.title: Pick a sublayer and a query
blocks: Chapter 9 built four masks from the token ids. Each RT block uses them in four attention sublayers, always in the order column, feature, neighbor, full, and then applies a feed-forward sublayer . Every attention sublayer has its own RMSNorm and its own four projection matrices . So the 4 blocks of the mini model hold 16 different attention sublayers, and the 12 blocks of the paper model hold 48 .

Pick one in the map. Each cell shows ‖Δx‖, the length of the update that the sublayer adds to the query’s residual stream in the live forward pass. Then pick a query token: the masked target by default, or any other cell of the context. The rest of this chapter and chapters 7 to 9 share this choice, so a token you inspected there is the query here.
The attention sublayers of the mini model, and the query token

For this query the Neighbor row of the map reads 0 in every block. No token in the context has the query’s row among its parents, so its row of the neighbor mask is empty, and an empty row gives an update of exactly zero . In the other three layers a token can always read at least itself .

sections.title: Seven steps through one sublayer
blocks: Each attention sublayer sits inside a pre-norm residual: the block computes x+MHA(RMSNorm(x)) . The norm applies to the sublayer’s input, and the raw output is added back to x. Chapter 11 looks at this placement more closely. Inside MHA, three linear maps without bias give the queries, keys and values, which are then split into heads. FlexAttention computes a masked softmax for each head, and a fourth map Wo mixes the concatenated head outputs . For head j and query token q:
ℓ is the layer (column, feature, neighbor or full), Mℓ its mask, and Mask(a;M)=a where M[q,k]=1, −∞ otherwise.

The paper writes attention for a single head, with queries and keys of dk numbers each and a divisor dk . With several heads, dk is the width of one head, the dhead of other chapters: 256 / 8 = 32 in the paper model and 64 / 4 = 16 here. The code passes no scale to FlexAttention, which then divides by the square root of the head width by default .

Two pieces of general Transformer background help with the steps. They come from the original Transformer paper rather than from RT . First, the three roles. A token’s query describes what it is looking for, each key describes what a token offers, and the score q⋅k measures how well the two match. The values are what the tokens hand over, averaged with the softmax weights. Second, the divisor. If the numbers in q and k were independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product would have variance dk. Wider heads would then give larger scores and push the softmax towards a single key, where its gradients are tiny. Dividing by dk brings the variance back to about 1.
The figure below walks through the sublayer one step at a time. Each step shows the live tensors on the left and the arithmetic, with this token’s numbers, on the right.

Every vector and number is read from the forward pass of the live context, computed in your browser. Use the player or click a stage; click any bar (or use ← →) to inspect a key. The accent triangle marks the query’s own position: in the column, feature and full layers a token may attend to itself .
Three things to watch as you step:
In step 3, head 1’s query uses all 64 numbers of h, but only its own 16 rows of Wq. The faded rows produce the other heads’ queries. In the code this split is the reshape "b s (h d) -> b h s d" .

In step 5, switch the layer while the query is the masked target. The column mask keeps the cells of the label column, the feature mask keeps the target’s own row and its customer, the neighbor mask keeps nothing, and the full mask keeps every real token .
In step 6, every blocked key gets a weight of exactly 0, because e−∞=0, so the allowed weights alone sum to 1 .

In the feature layer it reads its own row and the row of its customer. In the neighbor layer it reads nothing, because no row points to a task row, and in the full layer it reads every real token .

Among the attention layers, removing the column layer hurts zero-shot R² the most (22.8 → 11.9) , although for classification, the task type of the running example, the effect is small (70.1 → 69.8 AUROC) . When block 1’s column layer runs, each token is still its input embedding: a column-name term plus a value term, with no row, entity, time or position information . sections.title: Implementation note: FlexAttention and a dense loop
blocks: The paper implements the relational layers “with sparse attention masks, and compiled to efficient FlashAttention-based kernels using FlexAttention” . In every forward pass the code turns the four masks into FlexAttention block masks once, before the first block, and every block reuses them . A block mask lets the GPU skip the parts of the score matrix that a mask blocks entirely .

This site runs in your browser without a GPU, so its engine loops over each query’s allowed keys in plain TypeScript. The arithmetic is the same masked softmax: scores scaled by 1/dhead, blocked keys excluded, weights normalized over the allowed keys . A query with no allowed key, such as the masked target in the neighbor layer, has nothing to normalize. FlexAttention outputs 0 for such a row, and since Wo has no bias, the update is 0 as well . The checks below test these properties on the engine’s live forward pass:

736,992 blocked (query, key) pairs × heads: largest weight = 0 exactly
6,832 rows of weights with at least one allowed key: max |Σp − 1| = 4.5e-8

Checked on the live forward pass of this context. 85 of the 128 real tokens have an empty neighbor row. The column, feature and full rows of real tokens are never empty, since they always contain the query itself . Every empty row leaves its token unchanged, in every block . The sums differ from 1 only by rounding.

sections.title: The RT block and the residual stream
blocks: Attention is one sublayer. A block chains five sublayers: four attention layers (three relational, one full) and a gated feed-forward network. Each adds its result to a running vector per token. This chapter builds the block, stacks it, and follows the masked target through the whole stack with the live numbers of the trained mini model.

sections.title: One block, five sublayers
blocks: After the embedding of chapter 8, every token of the context is a vector of d = 64 numbers (256 in the paper). Inside the blocks the model only ever adds to that vector. Each sublayer reads the token’s current vector, computes an update, and adds it back: x←x+f(x) . The running vector is called the residual stream, and the identity path that carries it past every sublayer is the residual connection.

An RT block has five sublayers. The first four are attention layers, always in the order column, feature, neighbor, full, and the fifth is a feed-forward network . Each has its own RMSNorm and its own weights, so a block holds five RMSNorms, four separate attention modules and one feed-forward module .
One RT block, as the code runs it. Each line reads the x left by the line above.

Walk through a block below. The pulse follows one token, the masked target by default, and each box shows ‖Δ‖, the length of the update that sublayer adds in the live forward pass. Click a box to inspect it.
An RT block, with the live numbers of one token

For the target, the neighbor box stays at zero in every block. The neighbor mask lets a row read only the rows that point to it, and no row has a foreign key to a task row: task tables have no primary key, so their rows are never parents . The target has no key to read , so its attention output is 0, and since Wo has no bias, the update is the zero vector . instead: its neighbor row has 76 keys, so its neighbor update is not zero.

Line 83 sets the order the layers run in. The order in which __init__ lists them does not matter. Line 84 is the whole attention sublayer: normalize a copy, attend under this layer's mask, add the result. Line 85 does the same with the FFN.

sections.title: Pre-norm: where the norm sits
blocks: Every sublayer starts with an RMSNorm. It divides a vector by its root mean square and multiplies each dimension by a learned weight γi . Unlike LayerNorm, it subtracts no mean and adds no bias. The ε under the root is a small constant that keeps the denominator above zero.

The norm sits on the sublayer’s input. The sublayer reads RMSNormℓ(x), and its raw output is added to the stream . This placement is called pre-norm. The paper says RT follows LLaMA for “normalization, activations, etc.” , and LLaMA normalizes the input of each sublayer for training stability .
The paper’s Algorithm 2 puts the norm on the sublayer’s output instead, X←X+Norm(MHA(X;M)) . The code is pre-norm, and this site follows the code .

With the norm on the input, a sublayer always reads a vector of controlled length. However long x grows, the length of RMSNormℓ(x) depends only on the direction of x and the weights γ. The output is not normalized. It goes straight back into the stream, so an update can be as long as the sublayer makes it. Inside a block the stream itself is never rescaled, only added to.

The chart shows this for the target in the trained mini model. Its stream grows from ‖x‖ = 6.30 at the embedding to 14.79 after block 4 (blue), while every sublayer reads a copy whose length stays between 6.22 and 6.98 (orange). The updates have lengths from 0.28 to 2.44, and exactly 0 where a sublayer has no key to read. The final RMSNorm, norm_out, is the only norm applied to the stream itself. It brings the length to 6.63 before the decoders read it .

sections.title: SwiGLU: the feed-forward sublayer
blocks: The fifth sublayer is a gated MLP. The paper describes “gated MLPs with SiLU activation, as found in the LLaMA architecture”, with a hidden dimension of 1024 . In the code it is three linear maps without bias :

W1 and W3 map the normalized vector h from d = 64 to dff = 256 hidden units, and W2 maps back to 64. The paper model uses 256 → 1024 → 256. In both, the hidden layer is four times as wide as the stream, dff = 4d . The name SwiGLU joins Swish, another name for SiLU, with GLU, a gated linear unit . SiLU(W₁h) is the activation, and W₃h is a learned linear gate that multiplies it unit by unit.

The FFN works on each token separately. It mixes the 64 dimensions of one token’s vector and never looks at another token, so inside a block, information moves between tokens only in the four attention sublayers.
SiLU, the gate, and the hidden units of a live token

sections.title: The stack: 4 blocks here, 12 in the paper
blocks: The model is a stack of blocks with the same shape and separate weights, followed by one more RMSNorm, norm_out . The forward pass runs the blocks in sequence, hands each one the same four masks (built once from the token ids), and then applies norm_out . The paper model has 12 blocks of width 256 with 8 heads , and the mini model has 4 blocks of width 64 with 4 heads.
The forward pass, end to end

Counting every weight in model.py at the paper’s sizes gives 22,336,131 parameters, the “about 22M” of the paper . The frozen MiniLM text encoder is not included, because its 384-d embeddings are computed once, before training . The mini model has 535,491, of which 460,032 sit in the blocks. In both models the blocks hold most of the weights, and the attention matrices are the largest single group.

sections.title: How information can reach the target
blocks: In an attention sublayer, query q can receive from key k exactly when the mask allows the pair, and the feed-forward sublayer moves nothing between tokens. The masks are therefore a map of where information can flow . Whether the trained model uses a route is a separate question, which the attention weights shown on each hop of the tracer below only partly answer. In block order, the four attention layers move information like this:
Column: the target reads every visible label of its column directly, its own customer’s past labels and other customers’ alike. It cannot yet tell which are which.
Feature: the target and every past task row read their parent customer’s cells, so each of them now carries information about which customer it concerns.
Neighbor: customer cells read their child rows, the labeled task rows and the orders and reviews rows alike. This is where per-customer aggregates can form, “analogously to message-passing in GNNs” .
Full: unrestricted mixing among all non-padding tokens.
Stacking blocks composes these hops: what a customer gathered in block 1’s neighbor layer reaches the target in block 2’s feature layer. Pick a source token below and trace it.
Route tracer: from any token to the masked target
Three routes on the live context, through the relational layers only (full attention switched off):
a past label of the same customer: #20 train258·churn → B1 column → target
an order of this customer: #7 o70·order_time → B1 neighbor → #2 c35·name → B2 feature → target
a cell of another customer: #111 c74·name → B1 column → #2 c35·name → B1 feature → target

The last route starts in a column layer: the customer’s own cells read the same column of every other customer in the context, and the target then reads its customer in a feature layer. Column attention links rows that no foreign key connects. With full attention every token reaches the target in block 1, since the full mask connects every pair of non-padding tokens. In the paper’s words, full attention “enables long-range interactions in a fixed number of layers, independent of database or graph diameter” .

sections.title: Expressivity notes
blocks: If full attention can reach everything in one layer, why keep the three relational layers? Appendix E of the paper discusses what each layer adds to the expressive power of RT :
Column attention

“Removing column attention does not reduce expressivity, since global attention can emulate it. In particular, some global heads can learn to restrict attention to tokens from the same column by exploiting table and column name embeddings in their query–key construction.”
RT is just as expressive without it, yet in the paper’s ablation it is the layer with “the highest impact on zero-shot transfer” (Table 5 below).
Feature attention
“Feature attention is the only mechanism that explicitly groups cells into rows.”

Neighbor attention gives only partial row information, the paper adds. Cells of one row attend to the same neighbors, but that cannot tell rows apart reliably, especially in a table that no foreign key points to, whose rows have no neighbors at all .
Neighbor attention

“Similar to column attention, neighbor attention is not strictly required for expressivity, as feature and global attention together can simulate its effect. Feature attention exposes F→P links, which global attention can then leverage to infer P→F relationships.”
In the masks, neighbor is exactly the transpose of the parent part of feature : every neighbor edge in the tracer above has a feature edge running the other way.
Full attention

“Without full attention, information can only propagate one hop per layer, limiting expressivity to local message passing. By contrast, full attention enables long-range interactions in a fixed number of layers, independent of database or graph diameter.”
Switch full attention off in the tracer to see the one-hop-per-layer limit on the live context.
The paper leaves a full theory of RT’s expressive power to future work . For evidence it turns to the layer ablation of Table 5, which retrains the model with one layer type removed.

The head that matches the cell’s type gives a logit or a z-score, which becomes a probability or a number in the column’s own units. The chapter also covers the loss that training minimizes and the two metrics the paper reports.

sections.title: A final norm, then four decoders at every position
blocks: Chapter 11 followed the vector through the last block. The forward pass then applies one more RMSNorm, norm_out, to every position and hands the result to what the paper calls “cell decoders (also called prediction heads), one for each datatype” .

In the code the decoders are four nn.Linear layers in a dictionary, dec_dict. The number, datetime and boolean heads map the d-dimensional vector to a single value. The text head maps it to 384 values, the size of a MiniLM sentence embedding . Each one has a bias.

The forward pass applies every head to the whole sequence, so each position, padding included, gets four outputs . Only one of these values is ever used: the output of the head that matches the masked cell’s type, at the masked position . In the paper’s words, “the decoder to select for final prediction depends on the task type, or equivalently on the datatype of the masked cell” . Step through it in the live context:
From the last block to four predictions

All values come from the live forward pass of the mini model. The color of a cell shows the sign and size of one coordinate (blue negative, red positive). Pick another position to see that the four heads produce outputs there too; only the masked cell’s own type is ever read.

The figure below zooms out to the whole context. Each column is one position and each row one decoder. Switch the view to see how the loss picks its single value: for each type i, the code builds sem_type_mask = (sem_types == i) & masks, so a position counts only if its token has that type and is the masked cell . Every other output is multiplied by zero.
Every position gets all four outputs (128 positions)

One column per position of the context, in token order. Each row is one decoder, colored by its output (blue negative, red positive, scaled per row). The text head’s 384 outputs per position are left out. The column with the dashed outline is the masked target. Hover or tap a column to read it; clicking also selects it in the figure above.
yhat = self.dec_dict[t](x) is a (B, S, D_t) tensor: all positions at once.
The text head is never trained

Text cells are never masked. The paper masks only “cells in boolean or numeric columns” , and the code raises an error if asked to: raise ValueError("masking text not supported") . No text output enters a loss, so the text head gets no gradient . It runs at every position like the other heads and learns nothing.
Reading the prediction
At evaluation time the code reads the boolean head for classification tasks and the number head for regression tasks, at the positions flagged is_targets .

sections.title: Binary targets: from logit to probability
blocks: For a binary task the masked cell is a boolean, so the boolean head is read. Its output z^ is an unbounded real number, a logit. The code never turns it into a probability: the loss takes the logit directly , and so does the AUROC . To show a person a probability, apply the sigmoid :

In the live context, the seed is customer 35 (Anna Müller). The task asks: “Will the customer place no order in the next 30 days? (churn = true means no order in (t, t+30d]).” The boolean head outputs z^=−0.198, so σ(z^)=0.451: the model gives a 45.1% chance that churn is true. The hidden answer is false.
From logit to probability

The curve is σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z)). The filled dot is the boolean head’s output at the masked cell; the slider moves a hollow dot to explore the curve. A logit of 0 is a probability of exactly 0.5.

The label is still inside the masked token. Its boolean_values slot holds the true value, gated out of the input so the model cannot read it (chapter 7) . Like every boolean, that stored value is a z-score (chapter 4). If μ is the share of true values, true becomes (1−μ)/σ>0 and false becomes −μ/σ<0, so the sign alone recovers the class . That is why the paper writes the loss as BCE(1{r>0},r′) and why the evaluation converts labels with int(x > 0) .

sections.title: Regression targets: from z‑score to the column’s units
blocks: For a regression task the masked cell is a number, so the number head is read. Its output is a z-score, on the same normalized scale as the stored label . Each numeric column was z-scored with its own mean and standard deviation, and the Val and Test rows of a task table reuse the Train split’s statistics . Undoing the z-score gives the prediction in the column’s original units:
Like the sigmoid, this step only matters for display. Training and evaluation both stay in z-space .

The global task is binary, so here is a local preview of product-sales: the seed is product 1 (Mechanical Keyboard), and the task asks “How many units of the product will be ordered in the next 30 days?” The number head outputs z^=+0.147. With the Train statistics μ = 4.380 and σ = 6.412, that is y^=5.32 sales; the hidden answer is 6.
From z-score to original units

One axis, two labelings: z above, sales below. Because ŷ = ẑ·σ + μ is a straight-line map, every point has both readings. Gray bars: the 321 Train labels whose μ and σ define the scale. The violet line is the number head’s output at the masked cell; the black line is the hidden label.

sections.title: The loss, with numbers
blocks: Training compares the read output with the hidden label. As the paper puts it, “we apply HuberLoss(r, r′) for regression and binary cross-entropy loss BCE(1{r > 0}, r′) for binary classification. The overall loss is the mean over all masked cells in the batch” . Here r is the cell’s normalized value, so both losses work on z-scores . Pretraining and fine-tuning use the same objective .
Binary cross-entropy with logits
F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits takes the logit and the 0/1 target and computes −log⁡σ(z^) for a positive and −log⁡(1−σ(z^)) for a negative, rearranged so that no exponential can overflow :
Binary cross-entropy with logits, at the masked cell

Each curve is the loss as a function of the logit for one value of the label. The dot is the live prediction on the curve of the actual label. A confident wrong logit costs about |z|; a confident right one costs almost nothing.
Huber loss

Number targets use F.huber_loss with its default δ = 1, on the residual between the predicted and the stored z-score . Small errors are penalized like a squared error and large ones only linearly, so the gradient from a single cell never exceeds 1 in size. An unusual label, such as a product with a sudden burst of sales, pulls on the weights no harder than any other badly predicted cell.
Huber loss (δ = 1), at the masked cell

The solid curve is the Huber loss of the residual d = ẑ − z, both in z-space. Inside the shaded band (|d| < 1) it equals ½d², the dashed parabola; outside it grows only linearly, |d| − ½, so its slope never exceeds 1.
The mean over the masked cells of a batch
The code adds up the loss of every masked cell, type by type, and divides by the number of masked cells, loss_out / masks.sum() :

Each context has exactly one masked cell, so this is the plain mean over the contexts of the batch. No task, type or class gets extra weight . Pretraining shuffles the items of all its tasks into one list, so a batch can mix binary and regression cells :
A mini batch of 8 training contexts: one masked cell each

4 Train rows of customer-churn and 4 of product-sales, each with its own sampled context (epoch 0), run through one model (checkpoint pretrain-churn). Bars are the per-cell losses; the line is their mean, the number the optimizer minimizes. The batch is an illustration: these exact steps were never taken in training.

sections.title: Metrics: AUROC on logits, R² in z‑space
blocks: The paper scores binary tasks with AUROC and regression tasks with R² . The evaluation loop collects the read output and the stored label of every evaluated seed, then calls scikit-learn once per task and split . Each seed gets one context and “a single forward pass” , with no averaging over several contexts .
AUROC

AUROC is the area under the ROC curve. It also has a direct reading: pick at random one seed whose label is 1 and one whose label is 0. AUROC is the probability that the first gets the higher score, with ties counting half. Only the order of the scores matters. The sigmoid never changes the order of two logits, so AUROC on logits equals AUROC on probabilities, and the code can skip the sigmoid . The figure evaluates every seed of the split in your browser.
AUROC on the logits: how well the scores rank the two classes

Left: the ROC curve, true-positive rate against false-positive rate as the threshold sweeps down the logits. Right: every seed’s logit, split by its label. The violet threshold line and the violet dot on the curve move together. AUROC is the shaded area under the curve.
R² compares the squared errors of the predictions with those of the simplest possible predictor, the mean label yˉ of the evaluated seeds:

Predicting yˉ for every seed scores exactly 0, which the paper’s Table 2 calls the global mean baseline . A negative R² is worse than that. The code computes R² on z-scores. Converting labels and predictions to original units multiplies both sums by σ², so their ratio, and R², stay the same .
R² in z-space: how much of the labels’ spread the predictions explain

Each dot is one seed: its label against the number head’s prediction. Dots on the diagonal are perfect. The dashed line predicts the mean label ȳ for everyone, which scores R² = 0 by definition. Switching to original units rescales both axes by σ and leaves R² unchanged.
These are our mini model’s numbers on synthetic data. The paper’s own results are in chapter 16.

sections.title: One decoder per type, shared by everything
blocks: The whole model has a single number head and a single boolean head, shared by every column, table and database . The same handful of weights predicts the sales of a product, the rating of a review and, in the pretraining databases, the grade of a submission or the points of a driver. The output is read in the target column’s own z-space, as a number of standard deviations above that column’s mean . Nothing in the head itself says which column it is predicting. That information reaches it only through x^, which carries the column-name embedding of the masked token (chapter 8).
One output value, read in each target column’s own scale

Every target of every task in the four databases. The same decoder serves all the rows of one type: its output is a z-score of the target column (number rows) or a logit (boolean rows). Statistics are recomputed live from each database’s preprocessing.

Because the heads are shared, a pretrained model can answer for a column it has never seen. Our pretrained heads learned from the targets of SchoolDB, RacingDB and ForumDB, and are read on ShopDB without any weight update . One output scale can serve all these columns because each is z-scored on its own: over the rows that define its statistics, every regression target has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

sections.title: The whole pass on one page
blocks: A forward pass of RT answers one question: what is the value of one masked cell? Exactly one cell of the context is masked, the seed row’s target cell , and everything on this page leads to that one number. The map below lists the seven stages and the shapes that pass between them. Each section after it opens one stage on the live seed.
The whole pass at a glance

Shapes of what flows between stages, and the learned weights each stage uses (535,491 in all for this site’s model, including the text decoder that is never read). Click a stage to jump to it. The live column follows the seed chosen in stage 1.

All the figures share one followed token. It starts as the masked target, and you can follow any other token by clicking its row in any matrix or picking it from the list. Its row is outlined in every matrix and its numbers are written out next to the figure. Matrices show one small rectangle per entry: red for positive values, blue for negative, gray near zero, each on its own scale unless a figure says otherwise. Hover or focus any entry, or move through a matrix with the arrow keys, to read its value and how it was computed. Hover the shape under a matrix (rows × columns) to see what one row and one column stand for.

sections.title: Pick a task and a seed row
blocks: A forecasting task lives in a task table that “stores the forecasting labels, together with foreign keys linking to the relevant entities … and a timestamp specifying the prediction horizon” . RT attaches it to the database like any other table, and its rows are the seed rows . An autocomplete task seeds on a row of an ordinary table instead and masks one of its columns, after dropping the columns that would give the answer away .

A row can be a seed only if it has a value in the target column . For a forecasting task the seeds come from the chosen split of the task table; for autocomplete they come from the database table, whatever the split . Pick a task and a seed below, or keep the course’s running example.
The question the model will answer

These pickers change the simulation for the whole course, like the settings in the top bar. ShopDB is the held-out database: with the default checkpoints its tasks run zero-shot, while the other three databases were seen in pretraining.

The target’s type decides how the answer comes out at the end: a boolean target is read from the boolean decoder as a logit, a number target from the number decoder as a z-score . Chapter 3 builds the task tables and their splits.

sections.title: Sample the context
blocks: A database does not fit in one context, so the sampler gathers cells around the seed, row by row, until it has L = 128 of them (1024 in the paper) or runs out of rows . It follows four rules :
Parent rows, reached through foreign keys, come first, from a last-in, first-out stack: “F→P links are immediately followed” .
Otherwise the next row is drawn uniformly among the child rows with the lowest depth label .

A child row with a timestamp later than the seed’s is skipped, and at most w = 16 database children of each row are kept, chosen uniformly. Children in the seed’s own task table, which carry the labels, are never subsampled; rows of other task tables are skipped .
Each visited row adds its cells in order, and the sampler stops at exactly L, even in the middle of a row .
Sampling the context, one row at a time

A replay of the sampler’s recorded decisions for this seed. Each step visits one row and appends its cells to the context; the strip at the bottom fills up to L = 128. Click a token in the strip to follow it on the rest of the page.

For this seed the context holds 12 earlier labels of the same entity and 0 of other entities: unmasked cells of the target column, the in-context labels . Chapter 6 takes the sampler apart one decision at a time.

sections.title: Write the tokens
blocks: Each emitted cell becomes one token, written into flat arrays position by position: the row’s node id and its up to five parent ids, the table and column-phrase ids, the semantic type, the value slots and the flags . Positions left over after the sampler stops keep the padding defaults . The masked target still holds its true label in its value slot. Only its masks and is_targets flags mark it, and the input embedding puts a mask vector in place of that value .
The batch dictionary: 128 tokens, one row each

The official field names, in batch order. Click a row to follow that token on the rest of the page. Values are the stored model inputs (z-scores), not the raw cell values; the cell column is for reading only.

From here the fields split into two groups. The ids are compared between pairs of tokens to build the masks (stage 5) and are never embedded. The values become the input vectors (stage 4). Chapter 7 goes through the fields one by one.

sections.title: Embed every token
blocks: Every token starts as the sum of two 64-d vectors: one for its column, one for its value :

ci is the frozen MiniLM embedding of the phrase “<col> of <table>” and vi the token’s value: a z-scored number, datetime or boolean , or the MiniLM embedding of a text value . Each type t has its own linear encoder and its own RMSNorm. The masked cell gets its type’s learned mask vector mt in place of a value: “For masked cells, the value embedding … is replaced with a learned mask vector” . Padding gets the zero vector. Nothing encodes a token’s position in the context .
From batch fields to x₀ · Text lookups

One row per token, the followed token outlined. Hover any entry for its arithmetic; click a row to follow that token. Text embeddings are the frozen MiniLM vectors; everything after them uses the trained mini model’s weights.
Chapter 8 takes the embedding apart term by term, and chapter 5 shows what the frozen text encoder makes of the column phrases.

sections.title: Build the four masks
blocks: This is the only place where the links between rows enter the model . From the ids alone, the forward pass builds four boolean 128 × 128 matrices, one per attention layer : column (same column of the same table), feature (the same row and its parent rows), neighbor (the child rows) and full (everything) . Each is ANDed with “neither token is padding”, built once, and shared by every head of every block .
Four 128 × 128 masks from the token ids

Rows are queries, columns are keys, in token order; a filled entry means the query may attend to the key. The followed token’s row is outlined. Hover any entry to compare the four layers on the same pair; click it to follow the query token.
Chapter 9 explores who can see whom in each layer and why.

sections.title: Run the 4 blocks
blocks: The 128 × 64 matrix x₀ now passes through 4 blocks with separate weights (12 in the paper) . Inside each block, four attention sublayers run in the order column, feature, neighbor, full, then a SwiGLU feed-forward sublayer. Each is wrapped in a pre-norm residual: the sublayer reads a normalized copy of x, and its output is added back to x itself :

An attention sublayer projects the normalized rows to queries, keys and values with three 64 × 64 matrices and splits them into 4 heads of 16 dimensions. Each head scores every query against every key, sets the forbidden pairs to −∞, takes a softmax per row and averages the values with those weights; Wo then projects the concatenated heads back . The SwiGLU widens each token to 256 twice, gates one copy with the other and projects back . None of these layers has a bias. The player below steps through every operation of every block, 128 steps in all, and the sublayer grid jumps straight to any one of them.
Block 1 · Column attention · RMSNorm

Every matrix comes from the live forward pass of the mini model on this context, one row per token; the followed token’s row is outlined in accent. Hover or focus any entry to see the numbers it is computed from, and click a token row to follow that token. Signed values are red (positive) and blue (negative) around a gray zero, each matrix on its own scale; attention weights use the blue scale from 0.
Chapter 10 follows one query through one sublayer with bar charts, and chapter 11 follows one token’s vector through the whole stack.

sections.title: Decode and read the answer
blocks: After the last block one more RMSNorm, norm_out, normalizes every row . Then four linear decoders, one per data type, run at every position , and the one that matches the masked cell is read there: “the decoder to select for final prediction depends on the task type, or equivalently on the datatype of the masked cell” .
From the last block to the answer · Final RMSNorm
The same matrices as before, one row per token. The masked target’s row is where the answer is read.

For this task the answer is a logit; the probability is its sigmoid . The paper’s metric, AUROC, ranks the logits of many seeds directly . That is the whole pass, and no weight changed during it. The model never trained on ShopDB: everything it used about this database came through the context window . Chapter 12 covers the decoders, the losses and the metrics in depth.

sections.title: The same pass at the paper’s size
blocks: At the paper’s scale the context has 1024 cells gathered with w = 256, the matrices are 1024 × 256, the heads are 8 of 32, the SwiGLU is 1024 wide and there are 12 blocks: 22,336,131 weights against this model’s 535,491 . The map at the top of the page switches its shapes between the two.

sections.title: Pretraining, zero-shot, fine-tuning
blocks: Every chapter so far ran the model with trained weights. This one shows how they were made: pretraining that hides one cell per context, a database held out for testing, a one-cycle learning-rate schedule, a checkpoint chosen per task, and fine-tuning at the end. The figures come from this site’s own training run, shown next to the paper’s recipe.
What RT is trained to do: recover one masked cell per context, with one loss for pretraining and fine-tuning
What leave-one-database-out means, and why choosing a checkpoint on the target’s validation labels still counts as zero-shot
How the learning rate and Adam’s β1 change over a pretraining run
What our miniature run achieved on ShopDB, before and after fine-tuning, and what it cannot tell you

sections.title: One masked cell per context
blocks: Pretraining gives RT the same exercise it will face at test time. Take a seed row of some task, sample its context window (chapter 6), hide one cell, and ask the model to recover it. The hidden cell is always the seed’s own target: the label of a forecasting task row, or the target column of a row for an autocomplete task. There is exactly one masked cell per context, and every other cell, past labels included, stays visible .
masks marks the cells the loss is computed on; it is set to is_target, so one cell per sequence.

The model predicts that cell with the decoder of its type and is scored with the loss of that type: binary cross-entropy against 1{y > 0} for a boolean, the Huber loss with δ = 1 for a number, both on z-scored values. “The overall loss is the mean over all masked cells in the batch”, and “this formulation is used in both pretraining and fine-tuning” . Fine-tuning changes the data; the objective stays the same. Chapter 12 works through both losses with live numbers.

Which seed rows does pretraining use? It builds one dataset over every training task of every pretraining database, all on their training split . A forecasting task contributes the rows of its Train split; an autocomplete task contributes every row of its table that has the target cell . These items go into a single list with no balancing, so a task’s share of the training signal is its share of the rows . Step through the figure to watch one batch of our run come together.

Seed lists and contexts are computed live by this site’s engine, the same code that exported our training data. Tasks enter in proportion to their number of seed rows: autocomplete tasks, which use every row of a table, dominate .

In our run the four autocomplete tasks supply 78% of all items, because they use every row of their table (submissions, votes, results), while a forecasting task has one row per entity and timestamp. A batch therefore mixes databases, tasks, booleans and numbers, and every optimizer step averages its gradient over all of them. In the running example the masked cell is customer 35’s label in customer-churn. ShopDB never appears in pretraining: for it, the same exercise is the test.
The code behind the figure
From the task list to the batch loss, in the order the figure steps through. Pick an excerpt.
Every task tuple gets the split "train"; for autocomplete tasks data.py then resolves it to the whole DB table.

sections.title: Leave one database out
blocks: Zero-shot means “predicting new targets on a new RDB with a new schema, without weight updates. Information about the new RDB is available only at inference time, solely through the context window” . To test this honestly, the target database must stay out of pretraining. So the paper pretrains “separately for each target dataset on all tasks from all other datasets” : leave-one-database-out. RelBench has seven databases. rel-event is in every pretraining mix but never evaluated, “as it has been found to have temporal leakage issues” .
Counts are computed live by the engine. Forecast tasks contribute their Train split, autocomplete tasks every row of their table .
In the pretraining script the whole protocol is two list filters: train on every task whose database is not rel-amazon, and evaluate rel-amazon’s forecasting tasks on val and test .
That leaves 30 training tasks for rel-amazon; across targets, 29 to 33 (spec §9.1).

We do the same with four synthetic databases: SchoolDB, RacingDB and ForumDB for pretraining, ShopDB held out. ShopDB’s tables, column names and rows never reach the optimizer. The one thing it shares with the pretraining data is the frozen text encoder, which embeds every column phrase and string of every database the same way (chapter 5).

Why should anything transfer? The paper expects it “as databases share structural commonalities, e.g., dimension tables, fact tables, hubs and tripartite structures, as well as semantic similarities” . It later finds the main driver is the target entity’s own past labels . Our generators give every pretraining forecast task that property: an entity’s label in one window correlates with its label in the next, with lag-1 correlations from 0.42 to 0.73. A model that learns to read an entity’s history in SchoolDB can use the same skill on a ShopDB customer.

sections.title: The learning-rate schedule
blocks: The optimizer is AdamW with weight decay 0.1 and a peak learning rate of 10⁻³ . The schedule is PyTorch’s OneCycleLR . The learning rate η climbs linearly from 4·10⁻⁵ (the peak divided by 25) to the peak over the first 20% of the steps, then falls linearly to almost zero over the rest. The same scheduler moves Adam’s β1 the opposite way, from 0.95 down to 0.85 at the peak and back up .

Both runs use the same scheduler with T = total steps, so the curves have the same shape and only the step axis stretches. The paper’s curve is sampled every 250 steps; ours is logged at every update .

β1 is Adam’s momentum: how much of the previous update direction each step keeps. The one-cycle policy comes from Smith and Topin, who warm up to a large learning rate and then anneal it over most of training , and Smith recommends lower momentum while the learning rate is high . Because the scheduler sets β1 at every step, the β1 = 0.9 in the optimizer call below is never used.

sections.title: Our training run
blocks: Every trained number on the site comes from this run. It follows the paper’s recipe at a smaller scale: the same objective, optimizer, schedule and gradient clipping, with 4,001 steps of 32 contexts instead of 50,001 steps of 256. Each step runs the code’s train step. A forward pass computes the loss, the old gradients are cleared and a backward pass computes new ones. If the global gradient norm is above 1.0, the whole gradient is scaled down to norm 1. One AdamW update and one scheduler step finish it .

Every step is one batch of 32 contexts from all three pretraining databases, so the loss jumps with the batch’s mix of tasks; the moving average shows the trend. The norm is measured before clipping, as the code logs it .

The loss falls from about 0.45 in the first 100 steps to about 0.31 over the last 200, and it stays noisy from step to step because each batch draws a different mix of tasks. It never approaches zero: a context holds only so much information about its hidden cell, and our generators draw every label from a random process.

sections.title: Choosing the checkpoint, task by task
blocks: While it pretrains, the code evaluates the held-out database at step 0, every eval_freq steps and at every power of two. For each target task it keeps the checkpoint with the best validation metric and, at that moment, records the test metric of the same step . The numbers the run prints at the end, and the paper reports, are those recorded test metrics . Selection is per task because the authors “found significant overfitting during pretraining due to limited pretraining tasks” .
Both metrics are higher-is-better (AUROC on logits, R² in z-space), so one comparison serves both task types.
53 evaluations at step 0, every 100 steps and at every power of two, before that step’s update . The rule is a strict “greater than”, starting from −∞ .

In our run, customer-churn keeps step 2,500 and product-sales keeps step 600. One pretraining run gives one checkpoint per task. That is why the site ships a separate zero-shot checkpoint for each task, such as pretrain-churn and pretrain-sales, and why the “auto” checkpoint setting depends on the task. The validation curve also jumps between neighboring evaluations, by up to 3.4 AUROC points for customer-churn on its 71 validation seeds. With so few seeds, which step wins is partly chance. At the chosen step the test AUROC is 77.9; at the last step it would have been 79.1.

sections.title: Results on ShopDB
blocks: For each ShopDB forecasting task, the figure places five models on one axis: an untrained network, the EntityMean baseline, RT zero-shot, and RT fine-tuned on ShopDB’s Train split from a random init and from the pretrained checkpoint. Churn is scored by AUROC and sales by R², both in percent as in the paper’s tables.
Every RT number is the test metric recorded at the step with the best validation metric, as in the paper . EntityMean predicts the mean of the entity’s past labels, falling back to the Train mean .
On customer churn, zero-shot RT reaches a test AUROC of 77.9, above EntityMean (76.9) and above the untrained network (75.5). Validation gives the same order: 74.9 vs 71.3 vs 69.0.

On product sales, zero-shot RT reaches a test R² of 58.5, below EntityMean (74.8). Pretraining alone lifts it from −27.6 for the untrained network, without a single gradient from ShopDB. EntityMean is a strong baseline when counts persist over time. In the paper it beats RT on two of the eight regression tasks (item-ltv 54.2 vs 32.5, post-votes 43.7 vs 33.9) .

Fine-tuning, again selected on validation, reaches a test AUROC of 71.7 on churn and a test R² of 67.9 on sales when it starts from the pretrained checkpoint. From random init it reaches 66.3 and 49.1. Step 7 shows the curves behind these numbers.

Two limits apply to all of this. The test sets are small, 74 seeds for churn and 30 for sales, so differences of a few points are within noise. The next figure makes this concrete: untrained networks, which have learned nothing, already spread from 29.6 to 75.5 in test AUROC on churn, depending only on their random seed. The data are also simple and synthetic: three small pretraining databases and ten tasks, against the paper’s six real databases and about thirty tasks. Our numbers show that the mechanism runs end to end. They say nothing about how RT compares with other models.

Dots: PyTorch-default initializations after torch.manual_seed(s), s = 0…6. The filled dot, s = 0, is the starting point of our pretraining run. Vertical lines: the pretrained zero-shot model (blue) and EntityMean (gray) on the same split.

Why isn’t an untrained network at 50? Its output is a fixed but random function of the context, and the context carries information about the label, past labels included. On only 74 test seeds, some random functions happen to rank churners above loyal customers and others below. The average over initializations is still 50. PyTorch draws every initial weight and bias symmetrically around zero , so a network and its twin with the boolean decoder’s weights and bias negated are equally likely. The twin outputs the opposite logit for every seed and ranks every pair the other way round (AUROC 100 − x). Any single network is one draw from a wide distribution.
The metrics average over every seed. The next figure follows a single prediction instead: the running example’s context, passed through the three checkpoints of its task.

The tokens and masks are identical in the three cards; the decoder output at the masked cell changes only because the weights do. One context is an anecdote: the metrics above average over every seed of the split.

You can recompute every number in this section in your browser. The panel below rebuilds each seed’s context with the engine, runs the exported weights and computes the metric the way the code does: AUROC on raw logits, R² in z-space .

Contexts use L = 128, w = 16 and sampling seed 0, as in training, whatever the global simulation settings say . The browser runs this site’s TypeScript forward pass, which chapter 17 checks against PyTorch.

sections.title: Fine-tuning: pretrained vs random init
blocks: Fine-tuning trains on the target task itself, on its Train split only, with the same objective, a constant learning rate of 10⁻⁴ and no weight decay . Only the weights carry over from the checkpoint: AdamW starts fresh, with no warmup . The paper compares starting from the pretrained checkpoint with starting from random weights (which it calls untrained RT) and plots both against fine-tuning steps on a log axis .

Same axes as the paper’s Figure 3: fine-tuning steps + 1 on a log scale, the first point being step 0 . Rings mark the step each run would keep (best val). Evaluations at step 0, at every power of two and every 64 steps.

The pretrained run has a head start. It begins where zero-shot ends (sales test R² 58.5), while the random init begins at −27.6. The paper’s Figure 3 shows the same kind of gap: its untrained curves start below the bottom of the axes .

In its first updates the pretrained sales run dips, from 58.5 to 51.6 at step 1, before it climbs. The paper sees “a small dip in performance in the very early steps, which we conjecture might be due to the model transitioning from a zero-shot, in-context-labels- and semantics-driven regime to a data-driven prediction regime” .

Train long enough and fine-tuning overfits. ShopDB’s churn Train split has 601 rows, and 1,025 steps of 32 contexts revisit each one about 55 times. Switch the figure to “training loss”: the loss keeps falling, while the test AUROC peaks at 78.2 (step 8) and ends at 58.6. Validation selection keeps step 192, with a test AUROC of 71.7, below zero-shot (77.9). The paper’s per-task curves for the small rel-f1 tasks bend down the same way .
It loads a pretrained checkpoint, then trains and evaluates on a single target task, here rel-amazon’s user-churn.

sections.title: Names carry meaning
blocks: Every token’s input contains the embedding of its column phrase, such as “churn of customer-churn” or “price of products”, from the frozen text encoder . On an unseen database these names are the model’s only clue to what a column means. Shuffling them tests how much the model relies on that clue.

In the paper, shuffling column and table names lowers the mean zero-shot AUROC from 70.1 to 69.5 and the mean R² from 22.8 to 20.5: “wrong names lead to consistent degradation” . After fine-tuning the effect disappears (77.5 vs 77.2 AUROC).

Here the shuffle permutes the 384-dimensional phrase embeddings among the columns in the context, in one random cycle, so every column receives another column’s name. The phrase includes the table name, so table names move with it. The masks are untouched, because the sampler stores a column’s id (read by the masks) and its phrase embedding (read by the input layer) in two separate arrays:
col_name_idxs is the column id that the masks compare; col_name_values is the phrase embedding that the input layer reads. The shuffle permutes only the second.

sections.title: A shorter or a longer context
blocks: Attention cost grows with the context length L. Figure 4 of the paper takes a model pretrained at L = 1024 and evaluates it with shorter contexts: L = 256, 512, 768, 1024 . The paper sums it up: “RT’s performance degrades gracefully, showing a drop of only 4% absolute AUROC and 7% absolute R² with 25% lower time and 20% lower memory.” .

For a given seed row the sampler makes the same random choices whatever L is ; L only decides when it stops . So a shorter context is exactly the first L cells of a longer one, and shrinking L removes the rows the search reached last. blocks: The authors rank the components that enable zero-shot transfer “in order of importance” :
Time-series forecasting from past task rows for the target entity.
Column attention with the help of Relational Attention to generalize to new column distributions.

blocks: The earlier chapters showed how RT turns one masked cell into a prediction. This chapter collects what the paper measured: how well RT predicts on databases it has never seen, how quickly it learns once fine-tuned, which parts of the context and the architecture the transfer depends on, and what RT cannot do yet.

The limitations the authors name, and the few places where the released code differs from the paper

sections.title: Zero-shot classification
blocks: Zero-shot has a precise meaning in the paper: “predicting new targets on a new RDB with a new schema, without weight updates. Information about the new RDB is available only at inference time, solely through the context window” . In every column of Table 1 the target task is unseen during pretraining . The columns differ in what else the model has seen:
No: the target database was held out entirely. RT is pretrained on the six other RelBench databases (leave-one-database-out) .
Yes: starting from that model, RT continues pretraining on the target database’s other tasks. The target task itself stays unseen .
Maybe: the Gemma3 LLMs, whose pretraining data “is unknown, but likely includes similar public datasets” . They read the same context subgraph serialized as JSON, plus dataset and task descriptions .

The non-neural EntityMean baseline predicts the mean of the target entity’s past labels . Those past labels carry a lot of signal, which makes it a hard baseline to beat (the context ablations below come back to this). Random guessing scores 50.
Mean zero-shot AUROC over 10 binary tasks
Table 1 · p.8

Each stem starts at the random baseline (AUROC 50) and ends at the method’s mean, as printed. Circles: the target database was never seen (“No”). Squares: continued pretraining on the target database’s other tasks (“Yes”). The target task itself is unseen in every column . Hover a row for what the method is.

Among the methods that never saw the target database, RT (No) has the highest mean, 69.7, ahead of EntityMean (66.7) and Griffin (64.0); the largest LLM reaches 64.6. In the paper’s words, RT “attains the best average AUROC and is the only method to consistently beat the entity mean baseline” . Task by task the picture is more mixed: EntityMean is higher on 4 of 10 tasks (EntityMean vs RT: amazon · item-churn, 73.0 vs 70.9; amazon · user-churn, 64.4 vs 64.0; hm · user-churn, 64.4 vs 62.8; stack · user-engage, 83.5 vs 75.7).

sections.title: Learning efficiency
blocks: Zero-shot is the first point of a longer curve. “The key promise of pretraining is efficient adaptation to new datasets and tasks” . On each unseen task the paper fine-tunes for 33k steps at a constant learning rate of 10⁻⁴ with no weight decay , and compares pretrained RT with untrained RT, an untrained RDL-GNN and Griffin .
Figure 3, in words: fine-tuning curves on unseen tasks
Fig. 3 · p.7

The paper plots test AUROC and R² against fine-tuning steps + 1 on a log axis, up to 32k steps at batch size 256, averaged over the tasks that do not overfit . This panel does not redraw the curves; it marks only the numbers the paper prints or states.

Table 10 shows where that curve ends: every model fine-tuned on the full training set until it converges. Pretrained RT has the best mean on both metrics, AUROC 77.2 and R² 33.2 . On classification, RelGNN and RelLLM (77.1) come within 0.1 points and win several tasks; the paper notes that they “utilize custom setups for each task, whereas RT uses a single unified hyperparameter setup” . On regression the gap is wider: the next-best means are untrained RT (28.4) and untrained Griffin (22.6).

sections.title: What the context contributes
blocks: To find out where zero-shot transfer comes from, the authors keep the pretrained checkpoints and change the context: they shuffle the column and table names, remove the target entity’s past task rows (self labels), or remove other entities’ task rows (other labels) . They repeat each ablation with fine-tuning on the modified contexts . The matrix holds Table 4’s means; click any cell to see it task by task.
Context ablations
Tables 4 and 11 · p.9, p.22

Self labels dominate. Without them, zero-shot AUROC falls from 70.1 to 53.8 and R² from 22.8 to −5.5, worse than predicting the mean. “Zero-shot transfer is driven primarily by the model’s ability to leverage past labels of the target entity” . RT does more than average those labels, though: it beats EntityMean, which does exactly that . After fine-tuning, the ablations barely move the means, except that removing self labels still costs regression 6.5 points of R² .
If self labels drive transfer, tasks whose contexts hold none should not suffer when they are removed. The paper’s own label counts (Table 12) make this easy to check.
Where self labels exist, removing them hurts
Tables 12 and 11 · p.23, p.22

Each point is one task. Horizontal: how many past labels of the target entity the sampler put into a 1024-cell context, on average (the standard deviations are large; see the tooltip or the table) . Vertical: the change in zero-shot AUROC when those self labels are removed . The two tasks whose contexts hold no self labels at all, rel-trial study-outcome and study-adverse, do not change when they are removed.

The paper’s Figure 5 asks a follow-up question: without self labels, does pretraining still help fine-tuning? It compares fine-tuning curves of pretrained RT with and without self labels, and of untrained RT without them. The gap between the two runs without self labels is the transfer that remains . The authors conclude that RT does learn other transferable patterns, “but self labels do constitute the dominant share of transfer from pretraining even during initial steps of fine-tuning” .

Self labels exist because task-table prompting puts the entity’s past task rows within reach of the sampler, and column attention lets the masked cell read their labels. sections.title: What the architecture contributes
blocks: The architecture ablations retrain RT with one of the four attention layer types removed from every block, adding blocks to keep the parameter count constant .
Attention-layer ablations
Tables 5 and 13 · p.10, p.23

Column attention matters most for zero-shot transfer: without it, zero-shot R² drops from 22.8 to 11.9 . After fine-tuning, no ablation costs more than two points of mean R² , and on classification the differences are small in both settings . Full attention matters least: “removing full attention has the least impact in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings, even significantly improving the results on some tasks” .
Does the order of the layers matter?

RT’s block runs column → feature → neighbor → full attention, or “CFN” in Table 15’s letters (full attention always comes last, so the letters leave it out) . Table 15 trains every order, plus a variant that runs the three relational layers in parallel and sums their outputs . Zero-shot means span only 69.3–70.6 AUROC and 22.1–23.6 R²: “the specific order of relational attention layers is not critical to performance” .
Attention order, zero-shot
Table 15 · p.24
Masking more than one cell

RT as released masks exactly one cell per context, the seed’s target , and this site does the same. Table 14 pretrains with extra cells masked too, each with probability P(mask) and each adding to the loss . More masking lowers zero-shot R² (22.8 → 16.9 → 15.3) but raises fine-tuned R² (33.2 → 35.6 at 0.2, 34.4 at 0.4). The “no pretraining” column fine-tunes from random initialization.

sections.title: RT as a feature extractor, and the cost of context
blocks: Instead of fine-tuning all of RT, you can freeze it and train a small head on its output. The paper takes “the masked token representation before the decoder layer from a pretrained RT” and trains only a 2-layer MLP on it . Table 3 covers five classification and four regression tasks, so its means are not comparable with Table 10’s averages over all tasks .

The MLP on pretrained RT beats full fine-tuning on R² and comes within 1.6 AUROC points of it. Even untrained RT embeddings are “sometimes competitive, and much better than untrained GNN embeddings” .
