sections.title: Limitations
blocks: The authors name three limitations and one direction for future work.
No recommendation or link prediction
“Limitations of RT include inability to handle recommendation or link prediction tasks.”
RT casts every task as predicting one masked cell . Recommendation and link prediction ask which rows should be linked; the paper names supporting them as future work.
Ch. 3: tasks as masked cells →
Key column names are ignored
“it does not incorporate the names of primary-key and foreign-key columns, which often carry useful semantics.”
PK and FK columns never become tokens; they only define rows and links, so a name like customer_id is never embedded .
Ch. 2: feature vs key columns →
Two foreign keys to one table look alike
“RT also does not disambiguate between different foreign key columns.”
A row’s parents are stored as a bare list of row ids. Nothing records which key column each id came from. Try it below.
Ch. 9: the feature and neighbor masks →
Simple cell encoders
“more advanced cell encoders can be explored, including graph positional encodings, to enhance performance for supervised fine-tuning settings in large-data regimes.”
Today each value enters through one linear layer and an RMSNorm per type , and there are no positional encodings .
Ch. 8: the token embedding →
The paper’s example, made concrete: who bought, who sold?

An illustration of the example on p.10 (row ids are made up). The preprocessor turns each foreign-key value into a parent row id and pushes it onto f2p_nbr_idxs; the column name is dropped . The feature and neighbor masks then only ask whether a row is in that list . Swapping the two values reorders the list and changes nothing else the masks see.
.any(-1) reduces over the five parent slots: which slot matched is never used.
Scope of the evaluation

All results cover RelBench’s forecasting tasks. Autocomplete tasks are used in pretraining but are not part of the standard benchmark, and rel-event is skipped “as it has been found to have temporal leakage issues” . Each run pretrains on six databases .

sections.title: Where the code differs from the paper
blocks: Where the paper and its released code differ, this course follows the code . Most of the differences are small. The ones below change what RT computes or what its context holds, and each card links to the chapter that shows it.
Where the norm sits in a block
Ch. 11: The block & residual stream
Algorithm 2 normalizes after each sublayer: X ← X + Norm(MHA(X; M)).
Pre-norm: each sublayer reads a normalized copy of its input, x + MHA(RMSNorm(x)), and the feed-forward layer works the same way.
Which rows feed the normalization statistics
Ch. 4: From rows to cells
Values are normalized with statistics “computed on the training split”.
Only the task labels use training-split statistics. Database columns use all their rows, and datetimes share one z-score across all tables and splits.
How the sampler picks rows
Ch. 6: The context window
Algorithm 1 picks a random parent from the frontier, takes the child with the smallest hop distance, and caps the children of every row at width w.
Parents come off a stack, in a fixed order and before any child. Children are drawn at random from the shallowest non-empty depth, and only database rows are capped at w; task rows never are.
Labels from the seed’s own date
Ch. 6: The context window
Not discussed. The paper only says that “rows with timestamps later than the seed row are excluded”.
Rows with the seed’s own timestamp pass that filter, so other entities’ labels for the very date being predicted can sit in the context.
How many cells are masked
Ch. 14: Pretraining & fine-tuning
Masked token prediction, and Table 14 also masks extra cells with probability P(mask).
Only the target cell is ever masked, one per context.

sections.title: Glossary
blocks: Every term defined in this course, with its sources. Hover a dotted term anywhere on the site to see the same definition.
AUROC
Area under the ROC curve, the metric for binary tasks. RT computes it on raw logits; sigmoid probabilities would give the same value.
Autocomplete task
Predict a masked cell of an existing database column. The seed is a database row and no task rows enter the context. Columns that would give the answer away are dropped while sampling.
See also:
BCE with logits
The loss for boolean targets, against 1{z > 0}, where z is the z-scored label (z > 0 exactly when the label is true).
BFS width bound (w)
At most w database children are kept for each visited row, drawn at random after the temporal filter. Task-table children are never subsampled. The paper uses w = 256.
Cell token
One non-missing feature cell, represented by its value, its column name and its table name. RT’s input sequence is made of these, so a row becomes one token per feature value it holds.
Column attention
A token attends to every token of the same column of the same table. The masked label sees every visible label cell of its task.
Column phrase
The string “<column> of <table>”, e.g. “age of customers”. Its MiniLM embedding is how a token learns which column and table it belongs to.
See also:
Context window (L)
The L cell tokens the sampler gathers around the seed (L = 1024 in the paper). Sampling stops at exactly L tokens, even in the middle of a row, and pads the rest if it runs out of rows first.
Depth label
The number of hops from the seed to a row waiting in the sampler’s frontier (+1 per F→P or P→F hop). The next child row is drawn at random from the shallowest non-empty depth.
EntityMean
Baseline: the mean of the target entity’s past labels, falling back to the global training mean of the target column.
F→P link
The link from a row that holds a foreign key to the row it references, its parent. The sampler always follows these links first, with no time filter and no width limit.
Feature attention
A token attends to its own row and to its parent rows (the rows its FKs point to): row-wise attention after joining each table with its parents.
Feature column
Any column that is not a primary or foreign key. RT turns its non-missing cells into tokens (number, text, datetime or boolean).
See also: ,
Forecasting task
Predict an entity’s label over a future window (t, t+Δ] from data up to t, e.g. whether a customer places no order in the next 30 days.
Foreign key (FK)
A column holding the position of a parent row in another table. It produces no token, only links: the child records its parent (F→P), and the parent gets a link back to the child (P→F).
See also: ,
Full attention
Every non-padding token attends to every other one. The paper also calls it “global” attention.
Global node index

One integer id for every row of a database, task-table rows included: the offset of the row’s table plus its position in that table. Database tables come first, in alphabetical order, then the task splits (test, train, val).
Huber loss
The loss for number targets, computed in z-space with δ = 1: 0.5d² if |d| < 1, else |d| − 0.5.
In-context label
A visible label cell in the context: another row of the same task table (the target entity’s past rows or other entities’ rows), or for autocomplete, other rows of the target column.
See also: ,
Leakage columns
Columns that would give away the answer of an autocomplete task (columns_to_drop). Their cells are skipped for the seed row and for rows with the seed’s timestamp.
Leave-one-DB-out pretraining
Pretrain on all tasks of every other database, then evaluate zero-shot on the one held out. For each target task, the checkpoint with the best validation score is kept.
Mask vector mₜ
A learned vector for each sem type. It takes the place of the masked cell’s value term and is added as it is, with no RMSNorm.
Masked target cell
The single masked token of a context: the seed row’s label cell. It keeps its column name and type, but its value embedding is replaced by the learned mask vector.
See also:
Neighbor attention
A parent’s tokens attend to the tokens of its child rows in the context, much like message passing in a graph neural network. A row with no children in the context gets a zero update.
P→F link
The reverse of an F→P link: from a parent row to each child row that references it. A row can have a great many children, so the sampler filters them by time and keeps at most w of them.
Padding token
A filler position, flagged by is_padding, used when fewer than L cells were sampled. Its input is the zero vector, and every mask excludes it.
Permutation equivariance

Reordering the input tokens reorders the outputs in the same way: each token’s final hidden state moves with it, unchanged. RT has this property because each input vector depends only on the token’s own fields, and the masks depend only on ids.
See also:
Permutation invariance
RT has no positional encodings. Shuffling the tokens reorders the outputs the same way, so the prediction at the target stays the same.
See also:
Pre-norm residual
Each sublayer computes x + f(RMSNorm(x)): it reads a normalized copy of x, and its raw output is added back to x.
Primary key (PK)
The column that identifies a row. It produces no token and no link. In RelBench-style data its value is the row’s position, 0 to n − 1.
Coefficient of determination, the metric for regression tasks. Computed in z-space, it equals R² in raw units. Always predicting the global mean scores 0.
Relational attention

Multi-head attention restricted by a boolean mask built from the tokens’ table, column and row ids. The paper’s three relational layers are column, feature and neighbor attention; each block adds a full attention layer after them.
Relational database
A set of tables whose rows are linked through primary and foreign keys. RT reads it as a graph of rows, each row holding feature cells.
RMSNorm
y = x / √(mean(x²) + ε) · γ, with ε = 2⁻⁷ in RT. There is one before every sublayer, one after each input projection and one at the very end.
Row timestamp
The row’s time-column value in whole seconds. Only the sampler reads it, for its temporal filter.
Same-horizon rows
Other entities’ task rows with the same timestamp as the seed. The sampler skips only rows later than the seed, so these rows stay and their labels can appear in the context.
Seed row
The row whose target cell is predicted. Its cells come first in the context, and the BFS starts from it.
Self label
An in-context label of the target entity itself, from its past task rows. Removing them causes the largest zero-shot drop of any ablation in the paper.
Semantic type
Number (0), Text (1), DateTime (2) or Boolean (3), read off the column’s storage type: integers and floats are numbers, strings are text. Each type has its own encoder, decoder and mask vector.
SwiGLU feed-forward
FFN(h) = W₂(SiLU(W₁h) ⊙ W₃h) with no biases, 4× hidden width (256 → 1024 → 256 in the paper).
Task table
A table that holds the prediction task: a timestamp, a foreign key to the entity and the label. It is attached to the database as an ordinary table, with Train, Val and Test splits.
See also:
Task-table prompting
Giving RT a task by attaching its task table to the database. Its rows are the seeds, and the same task’s past rows, reached through the entity, bring visible labels into the context.
Temporal filter
A P→F child row is skipped when its timestamp is later than the seed’s. Equal timestamps pass, and parents are never filtered.
Text encoder
The frozen sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L12-v2 model (384-d, mean pooled, unit norm). It embeds column phrases, table names and text cell values once, ahead of time.
Time column
The one datetime column a table may declare. Its cells are ordinary datetime tokens, and its value also gives the row the timestamp that the sampler reads.
See also:
z-score normalization

Numbers and booleans are standardized per column as (v − μ)/σ. Datetimes share one mean and one standard deviation across the whole database. Task labels use statistics from the Train split, database columns use all their rows.
Zero-shot

Predicting on a database (or task) the model was never trained on, with no weight updates. The new data enters only through the context window. The checkpoint is still chosen on the target task’s validation split.

sections.title: Two halves: built once, run on every change
blocks: The offline half of the site ran once, on a CPU. It generated four small databases, embedded every string with the frozen text encoder, then trained the model and checked it. Its results are plain files in public/data/.

The online half runs in your browser whenever you change a setting. It regenerates the database, preprocesses it, samples a context window and runs the forward pass with the shipped weights and embeddings. No server computes anything.

Both halves use the same TypeScript preprocessing and sampler. That code built the training contexts offline, and it builds the live context here. So the model was trained on the same kind of token sequence the chapters show, and there is no second sampler that could drift from the first. Click a stage, or press play, to see what it does and what its numbers are right now.
The pipeline, stage by stage

Cards marked “shared code” run the same TypeScript in both halves. The dashed band holds the committed files that carry the offline results to your browser. Every number in the panel is live: read from those files or computed on this page.

sections.title: Three implementations of one function
blocks: A browser cannot run the official model: it is PyTorch code that needs FlexAttention, a compiled attention kernel . So the model exists here three times, and the checks connect them in a chain.
The official class RelationalTransformer from rt/model.py at the paper-era commit, run unmodified except for one pinned setting (RMSNorm ε, below). It is used only as the reference.
A PyTorch port with the same module and parameter names, so a checkpoint loads into either class. It swaps FlexAttention for dense masked attention and trains the model.
The browser engine, plain TypeScript, which runs every forward pass on this site.
What was compared with what
Bounds from public/data/verification.json, written by the verification step of the pipeline.

Why are the differences not exactly zero? Every value is a float32, which keeps about seven significant digits. The implementations add the same products in different orders (blocked matrix kernels in PyTorch, plain loops in TypeScript). Floating-point addition is not associative, so the last bit or two can differ. A difference near 10⁻⁶ on activations of size one to ten is a few float32 steps, while a real bug, such as a wrong mask entry or a missing norm, moves values by 10⁻² or more.
Run the parity test in your browser

python/parity.py exports real contexts together with every intermediate activation of the PyTorch model. The test suite then rebuilds each context with the TypeScript engine and compares the two forward passes stage by stage. The button below runs the same checks on your machine, with the weights your browser already loaded.
The trained-weights parity test, live

Each dot is the largest difference over all values of one stage: the input embedding x0, the output of each of the 20 sublayers (four attention layers and the feed-forward network in four blocks, numbered from 0 as in the fixtures), the final norm, the decoders, the loss and the prediction. The gray tick marks one float32 step at that stage’s largest value. Dots near their tick are rounding.
Every checkpoint against the official class

The chain holds only if the port equals the official class. parity.py loads each exported checkpoint into both, runs them on the same batch of real contexts from all four databases, and compares every decoder output and the loss. The official class runs its compiled FlexAttention on CPU.
TypeScript vs PyTorch on every fixture, from the last full run
The sampler, rebuilt independently

The forward-pass checks start from contexts built by the TypeScript sampler, so the sampler needs its own check. A separate Python program re-implements pre.rs, fly.rs and the masks directly from the Rust and Python sources , rebuilds thousands of contexts from the raw databases, and compares every token, the order in which rows were visited, and the masks. It uses an exact copy of the site’s random-number generator, so both programs make the same random draws.
Independent re-implementation of preprocessing, sampler and masks
The test suite

The unit tests pin down the behavior the spec describes: preprocessing statistics on the spec’s toy database, the sampler’s invariants (one target, the seed first, parents before children, the temporal filter, the width bound, the hard stop at L), the masks of the spec’s worked example, the forward pass against PyTorch, and properties of the generated databases. Every title below is read from the test files themselves.
Every test, as written
The specification and its adversarial check

The paper and the paper-era code were first distilled into a technical specification, the “spec” cited throughout this course, and the engine was written against it. Every non-trivial fact in it carries a citation: a file and line of the official code, a page of the paper, or a small script that checked it. The counts below are read from the spec’s text.

Then reviewers with three lenses (model, data, training) tried to break it. Each proposed correction was re-checked against the code, the paper and the PyTorch source, and the outcome was logged in §14 . Questions that could not be settled are listed as open in §13 rather than guessed .

sections.title: What is scaled down, and what is different
blocks: Scale is the only thing this site changes on purpose. Every operation, from the preprocessing formulas to the decoders, follows the paper-era code. A few other differences come from running in a browser on a laptop. The badge on each card says how far a difference reaches: the same operations at a smaller size, only the rounding, different random draws, or different learned numbers.
Model size
same operations
Paper
d = 256, 8 heads, 12 blocks, 22,336,131 parameters
This site
d = 64, 4 heads, 4 blocks, 535,491 parameters
The same modules, with narrower tensors and fewer blocks. Both parameter counts are computed here from the module shapes of model.py, and the paper’s count matches its “22.3M” .
Context size
same operations
Paper
This site

The sampler is the same algorithm at any (L, w); the cross-check above runs it at four settings, the paper’s among them . This site’s databases are small, so a short context already reaches the seed’s neighborhood.
Data
different numbers learned
Paper
RelBench: 7 databases, pretraining on the 6 not under test
This site
4 synthetic databases, pretraining on the 3 that are not ShopDB
Same protocol: leave one database out . The learned weights and every metric are this site’s own, and they are never plotted on one axis with the paper’s tables.
Precision
rounding only
Paper
bfloat16 weights and optimizer state , cell values and text embeddings ; RMSNorm ε = 2⁻⁷
This site
float32 throughout, embeddings included; RMSNorm ε pinned to 2⁻⁷
float32 keeps 24 significant bits where bfloat16 keeps 8, so the site’s numbers are closer to the exact result. ε is pinned so that RMSNorm divides by the same √(mean x² + ε) as in the paper’s runs .
Random numbers
different random draws
Paper
Rust StdRng (ChaCha12), seeded with epoch + seed row + seed
This site
xoshiro128** with the same seed formula, drawn at the same points

Wherever the sampler draws (which child rows to keep, which frontier entry to expand), the two generators pick different rows, so a given context is not bit-identical to Rust’s. The distribution over contexts is the same . The audit below shows what the draws decide.
Attention kernel
rounding only
Paper
compiled FlexAttention with block masks
This site
dense masked softmax (PyTorch port); per-query loops over allowed keys (browser)

All three compute the same function. The scores are scaled by 1/√d_head, the softmax runs over the allowed keys only, and a query with no allowed key outputs 0 . Only the order of floating-point additions differs, and the figure below checks it on the live context.
Training budget
different numbers learned
Paper
50,001 steps × 256 contexts × 1024 tokens on 8×A100, about 2 hours
This site
4,001 steps × 32 × 128 tokens on a CPU, 19 minutes
The paper’s model sees about 800 times more tokens (1.3 × 10¹⁰ vs 1.6 × 10⁷). The optimizer, schedule shape and selection rule are the same .
Evaluation sets
different numbers learned
Paper
at most 10,240 seed rows per split and task (40 batches × 32 seeds × 8 GPUs)
This site
71 / 74 customer-churn rows (val / test), 6 ShopDB sets in all

The official code stops evaluating after 40 batches per GPU, so it scores a fixed subset of each split . This site’s splits are tiny and evaluated in full, so a gap of a few AUROC points between two checkpoints is within noise.
One function, three kernels

Attention is where the three implementations look most different. All three compute the paper’s masked softmax, softmax(Mask(QKᵀ; M)/√d_head)·V with −∞ where the mask is 0 . FlexAttention receives the boolean mask as a block mask and treats masked scores as −∞ . The port computes all S × S scores and fills the masked ones with −∞. The browser engine keeps a list of allowed keys for each query and computes the softmax and the weighted sum over that list only.

Some queries have no allowed key at all. In the neighbor layer, this happens to every cell whose row has no child rows in the context. A plain dense softmax would divide 0 by 0 there and return NaN, but all three implementations output 0: FlexAttention’s compiled kernel replaces the zero sum by 1, the port zeroes these rows explicitly, and the engine skips them . The figure recomputes one sublayer of the live forward pass the dense way and compares its weights with the engine’s, query by query.
Dense softmax vs the engine’s, on the live context

Each strip has one cell per key position of the live context (gray = padding). Raw scores use the diverging scale (blue negative, red positive). Weights use the blue sequential scale, relative to the row’s largest weight; a weight of exactly 0 stays blank, and red marks NaN. Hover a cell to read its values, and use the arrows to step through the query positions. The figure uses the live context, so it follows your simulation settings.
What the random numbers decide

The official sampler seeds Rust’s standard generator with epoch + seed row + seed . This site uses a different generator with the same seed formula, and it draws at the same two points of the algorithm, with the same ranges. As the spec notes, bit-exact parity with Rust is not needed: any seeded generator gives the same distribution over contexts . What changes is which rows a given draw selects. The figure shows where the sampler drew in the live context.
Where the sampler used random numbers in the live context

sections.title: Who builds the task table, and how can it hold labels in a zero-shot setting?
blocks: When are the task tables created? If their cells are used in the inference step, these tables need to pre-exist to feed the transformer, right? How will they pre-exist and already have data in them if this is a new table that is being created now, and how does the algorithm know how to build these tables and populate them without knowing the context, being used in a completely zero-shot new dataset?

RT never builds a task table. It is input data, prepared before RT runs by whoever poses the prediction task: in the paper, RelBench’s task code fills every row with a label computed from what already happened in the database. The one unknown label, the seed’s, is masked. “Zero-shot” means no weight updates on the new database; you still have to say what to predict, and that task’s history reaches the model through the context window.

sections.title: RT reads task tables; it never makes them
blocks: A task table is part of the input, like the database’s own tables. It exists before preprocessing starts. The paper describes it as a table that “stores the forecasting labels, together with foreign keys linking to the relevant entities (e.g., user IDs or item IDs) and a timestamp specifying the prediction horizon” , and RT attaches it to the database: “For each task, we attach a dedicated task table to the database. Only one task table is active at a time … from the model’s perspective task tables are treated as ordinary relational tables” .
In the official code the order of events is:

Download. scripts/download_relbench.py asks RelBench for every dataset and every task. A task arrives as three ready-made files, tasks/<task>/train.parquet, val.parquet and test.parquet, labels included .

Preprocess. pre.rs reads db/*.parquet and tasks/*/*.parquet in one loop and turns both into rows and cells the same way. A task file becomes a table named after the task folder, of type Train, Val or Test .
Sample and predict. The sampler takes seed rows from that table and builds a context around each one .

No step computes a label. The repository reads the labels from these files; its only hard-coded edits to task tables cast some label columns to booleans (nonzero becomes true) and drop a stray index column .

sections.title: Who fills the rows: the task definition, run over the database’s past
blocks: RelBench does. A RelBench task is a small piece of code: an entity table, a time column, a target, a window length Δ, and a make_table(db, timestamps) method. For each timestamp t, it lists the active entities and computes each one’s label from what happened in the window (t, t + Δ] . For rel-f1/driver-dnf it is a SQL query: a driver gets did_not_finish = 1 when one of their race results in the next 30 days is not a finish.

The timestamps come from two cutoffs fixed by the dataset. Training rows step back from the validation cutoff in steps of Δ until the start of the data; validation and test rows sit at their cutoffs . RelBench refuses to build a split whose window would run past the end of the recorded data (“insufficient aggregation time”).

So a task table is a summary of history. Each label describes something that has already happened and is recorded in the database. That is why a table “created now” can be full of labels: it is created from the past. Even the test labels are on disk, and RT reads them, because the evaluation compares predictions with them .
ShopDB’s customer-churn task table, filled from the orders that already happened
The same figure as in chapter 3. Every label is a count over the orders table in the window after the row’s timestamp: nothing is predicted while the table is built.

sections.title: The one label that is unknown is masked
blocks: The label the model must predict is the seed row’s own. The sampler marks exactly that cell as the target and the mask . The model then replaces its value with a learned mask vector: the value encoder is multiplied by ~masks, the mask embedding by masks . The true value never enters the forward pass; only the loss and the metrics read it.

sections.title: Then what is “zero-shot” about it?
blocks: The paper defines zero-shot relational learning as “predicting new targets on a new RDB with a new schema, without weight updates. Information about the new RDB is available only at inference time, solely through the context window” . The definition is about the weights: none of them were trained on the new database or, in the paper’s experiments, on any table of it. It does not say the task needs no definition. Someone still decides what to predict (which entity, which outcome, which horizon), and the task table is how that decision is written down .
The model is never told what the task means. Everything it gets is cells in the context:
the target cell carries its column phrase, such as “did_not_finish of driver-dnf”, embedded as text like every other column name ;
its type picks the output: a boolean target is read as a logit, a number as a z-score ;

the context brings in earlier rows of the same task table, with their labels visible. From the seed, the sampler goes up to the entity row, then down to that entity’s other task rows with timestamps at or before the seed’s . These are the in-context labels.

The paper is explicit that this is not few-shot prompting: “While task rows provide ‘in-context labels’, our setting is not few-shot as explicit subgraph-label pairs are not required” . The labels are just more cells that the attention can read.

sections.title: And if the task has no history at all?
blocks: Then there are no past labels to put in the context, and the paper’s numbers say to expect little. Removing the target entity’s own past labels (its self labels) drops mean zero-shot AUROC from 70.1 to 53.8 . On rel-trial/study-outcome, contexts contain no labels at all (0 ± 0 per context) , and RT’s zero-shot AUROC is 51.8, next to the 50.0 of random guessing . The batch mode of the playground (chapter 15) runs the same removal on this site’s model.

The code also needs some history before it can run. Validation and test splits copy their normalization statistics from the task’s training split, so a task without a training split stops preprocessing with a panic .

sections.title: Autocomplete tasks need no task table
blocks: The other task family avoids the question entirely. An autocomplete task predicts a column that already exists, such as a review’s rating. The seed is the database row itself, its cell in that column is masked, and the in-context labels are the same column’s values in other rows that the sampler reaches. No task-table row ever enters such a context . See chapter 3 for both families on ShopDB.
